PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m grateful to colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20 for the very clear laying out of the sequi-jigsaw. Pe-, Di-, Ca-, Re- are unmistakable and quodque fit ex illis is unambiguously a charade built out of them. Where I keep getting stuck is not the material but what the second half of the verse is actually demanding the fur do, and what sequatur is doing to the order in which the verse names the pieces.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is a normal sequi construction with an accusative of the term that is followed. Didonis prima is nominative, the subject of sequatur, Penelopes primam is accusative, the thing it is made to follow. The verse puts the accusative first for emphasis, so in the linear order in which the riddle names the two terms we have Pe- named first and Di- as the subject that is made to follow it. It is the subject-accusative government that matters: the follower is Didonis prima, the followed is Penelopes primam. The same ellipsis governs et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi. With sequatur understood the nominative subject is syllaba prima Remi and the accusative it follows is primam Cadmi. The instruction is therefore that the Remus piece is made to follow the Cadmus piece.

In the order the verse actually names the four pieces that is Di-Pe and Re-Ca in the naming order, i.e. Di Pe Re Ca in the linear presentation of the four terms. That is DIPERECA, the letter stock of deprecare/deprecari, preces dare.

That resolves the dabis problem that several of us have been flagging. quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The fur is told dabis mihi the thing made from the pieces. Deprecari is literally preces dare, to give entreaty, to pray for mercy, to beg pardon. That is a thing that can be handed over, and it fits deprensus in horto with the deprensus/deprecare word-play the tradition loves. Pedicare/pedicari is something suffered or inflicted: you are made to pedicari, you do not dare pedicare to an owner. Dabis mihi wants a transferable datum, and preces are a datum.

The mixed wording prima / syllaba prima also points in this direction. If prima always meant ‘first syllable’ why is syllaba written out only for Remi and not for Penelope, Dido and Cadmus? A mixed littera/syllaba play is the usual way this kind of riddle signals a reversal of the surface concatenation.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re can be written on paper and the school tradition certainly quotes pedicare with its foot-fetter stocks sense and the later vulgar gloss. The semantic dispersion we are seeing right now — fetter/stocks vs penal sodomy vs ‘pay a fine’ — is a symptom of the strain of forcing pedicare into a dabis mihi clause. Deprecari gives one coherent classical verb, it respects the subject-accusative order of sequitur, it makes dabis mihi literal, and it gives the caught thief the penalty he can actually perform: he will be made to deprecate, to give preces for pardon, by which his culpa is luenda. That is the poena the syntax asks for.

3.text:
The two hemistichs are a single sequi-jigsaw with sequatur understood in
the second.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = Didonis prima nom. sequitur
Penelopes primam acc. The subject is the follower and the accusative is
the term that is followed. Penelopes primam is therefore put first and
Didonis prima is made to follow it

Pe- + Di- = Pe-Di

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* with sequatur understood in
parallel = syllaba prima Remi nom. sequitur primam Cadmi acc. The first
syllable of Remus is made to follow the first of Cadmus

Ca- + Re- = Ca-Re

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena
culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur deprensus in horto the patient of the
verb that is built out of the four pieces. The form that is imposed on him
is the passive pedicari.

Pedica is classically the foot-fetter, the stocks. Pedicare is to fetter,
to put the feet in the pedicae, to shackle / put in the stocks, the
ordinary corporal foot-punishment. That is the hac poena by which the
culpa of the fur in horto is to be luenda: the thief caught in the garden
is to be pedicatus, to suffer pedicare, to be fettered/shackled in the
pedicae.

That is the literal classical sense on which the school-book charade is
built. In the medieval scholastic reception the same Pe-Di-Ca-Re
pedicare/pedicari is notoriously vulgarised as the familiar garden-thief
joke, pedicari = to be made the passive partner, to ‘pay with his arse’,
the obscene gloss of the same pedicare punishment.

public_text.1:
The charade is a sequi-jigsaw and the order is given by sequatur in the text as it is normally quoted.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*. The nominative *Didonis prima* is the subject of sequatur and *Penelopes primam* the accusative it is made to follow. In the school parsing the instruction is read in the surface order Pe- followed by Di-: Pe- + Di- = PeDi.

The second hemistich is parallel with sequatur understood:
*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*. The nominative *syllaba prima Remi* is made to follow the accusative *primam Cadmi*. In the surface order Ca- followed by Re-: Ca- + Re- = CaRe.

PeDi + CaRe = Pe-di-ca-re.

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore *pedicare* and

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

makes the fur deprensus in horto the patient of the verb, the passive *pedicari*.

*Pedica* is classically the foot-fetter, the stocks. *Pedicare* is classically to fetter, to put the feet in the pedicae, to shackle / put in the stocks, the ordinary corporal foot punishment. That is the hac poena by which the culpa of the garden thief is to be luenda: the thief caught in the hortus is to be pedicatus, fettered / put in the stocks.

That is the literal classical sense on which the school-book *fur in horto pedicari* charade is built. In the medieval vulgar reception the same Pe-Di-Ca-Re formation is quoted in the familiar obscene gloss *pedicari* = to be made the passive partner, to be ‘paid with his arse’, the notorious garden-thief joke for the same *pedicare/pedicari*.

The DiPeReCa → deprecare / deprecari / PERDICAE reading is syntactically neat on *dabis mihi* and on the strict subject-accusative order of sequi, and it keeps the deprensus/deprecare echo. It does, however, require inverting the subject-object order of sequitur as the text is normally printed and it makes pedicare the etymologically transparent word the riddle builds out of Pe-, Di-, Ca-, Re-. On the conventional school parsing the punishment named by the riddle is pedicari, fettering in the pedicae / stocks, traditionally glossed in the school tradition as penal sodomy, ‘to pay with his arse’.

public_text.9:
I’ve been following the Pe-Di-Ca-Re material all round and it is certainly there in the names, and the school-book *pedicare/pedicari* gloss is the one most of us learned first. I’m still uneasy about how the threat is actually formulated, and that unease is what keeps pulling me back to the case order of *sequatur* and to *dabis mihi*.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is being read in the room as “let Di- follow Pe-”, but syntactically *Didonis prima* is nominative and *Penelopes primam* is accusative. With *sequi* the nominative is the follower and the accusative is the thing followed. The verse therefore names the Dido piece first as the subject and the Penelope piece second as the object it is made to follow. In the linear order the riddle names them we get Di- before Pe-.

The second hemistich is parallel by ellipsis: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]*. The subject is *syllaba prima Remi*, nominative, the accusative it follows is *primam Cadmi*. The verse names Re- before Ca-. That is the linear naming order Di Pe Re Ca.

That is not just a reordering exercise. It matters for the second half of the riddle:

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

The caught thief is told he will *dabis mihi* the thing made from the pieces. *Dabis mihi* wants a transferable thing. *Deprecari / deprecare* is literally *preces dare*: to give entreaty, to pray for mercy, to beg pardon. That is something you can hand over, and it matches the *deprensus / deprecare* echo the tradition loves for a thief caught in the *hortus*.

*Pedicare / pedicari* is what is suffered, what is inflicted on the patient. You are *pedicatus*, you are fettered in the *pedicae* or, in the medieval vulgar reception, you are made the passive partner. You do not *dare pedicare* to an owner; you suffer it. That is exactly why the *pedicare* camp keeps splitting in front of us between fetter/stocks, the late vulgar sodomy gloss, and a generic ‘pay a penalty’ reading. The meaning is being stretched to accommodate *dabis*.

The mixed wording also nags: *primam* for Penelope and Cadmus, *syllaba prima* for Remus. If *prima* meant ‘first syllable’ uniformly we would expect the same formulation throughout. The explicit *syllaba* for Remus suggests a deliberate littera / syllaba play and supports reading the case government as given.

Once the subject-accusative order of *sequitur* is kept and the literal *dabis mihi* requirement is kept, the eight letters the verse actually names in the order it names them are Di Pe Re Ca, the deprec- stock. A poena you can be made to *dare* is to be made to deprecate, to give preces for pardon, and that is a coherent atonement for a *fur deprensus in horto*. That is the reading that keeps both the charade and the syntax of the threat intact.
public_text.13:
I’m broadly with the school reading in that the four names are the material and that the riddle is a *sequi* charade. Penelope Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-, Remus Re- are unmistakable and *quodque fit ex illis* is meant to be built out of them. Pe-Di-Ca-Re can be written on paper and the *fur in horto pedicare/pedicari* tradition is real, with *pedica* the foot-fetter/stocks and the later vulgar gloss everyone is citing.

Where I keep getting stuck is the syntax the verse actually gives us and what *dabis mihi* can take.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is a normal *sequi* construction. The nominative subject of *sequatur* is *Didonis prima*, the accusative it is made to follow is *Penelopes primam*. The subject is the follower. In the linear order in which the riddle names the two pieces we therefore get Di before Pe. The second hemistich is parallel by ellipsis: *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* with *sequatur* understood. The nominative subject is *syllaba prima Remi* and the accusative it follows is *primam Cadmi*. So in the order of naming we get Re before Ca.

That is Di-Pe-Re-Ca in the order the verse names them, D I P E R E C A, the letter stock of the *deprec-* stem.

That matters for the threat:

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

*Dabis mihi* wants a transferable thing. *Deprecari/deprecare* is literally *preces dare*, to give prayers, to entreat for mercy, to beg pardon. A *deprecatio* is a thing you can hand over to an owner. *Pedicare/pedicari* is a thing you suffer or are made to suffer — you are fettered in the *pedicae*, you are made the patient of the penalty. You do not *dare* someone being fettered to them. The verb *dare* here pushes us toward a verb of giving, not of suffering.

The mixed wording *primam* vs *syllaba prima* also points the same way. If *prima* meant ‘first syllable’ uniformly, why is *syllaba* made explicit only for Remi? The variation is the classic littera/syllaba play and it sits comfortably with the DiPeReCa ordering.

I’m not denying the Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation exists; the school tradition certainly quotes it. The point is that the case government of *sequatur* and the semantics of *dabis mihi* make the reading that respects the subject-accusative order and the give-me requirement much more coherent. *Deprecari*, with the deprensus/deprecare echo the riddle loves, is a single classical verb meaning to be made to give preces, to entreat pardon — a penalty you can literally be made to *dare mihi* for being caught in the hortus, and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* reads as the atonement by supplication.

The visible split in the *pedicare* camp between fetter/stocks, generic ‘pay a fine’, and the later vulgar passive gloss is, I think, the symptom of that syntactic mismatch. Keep the four pieces, keep the charade, keep *sequatur* as written, and the coherent poena the verse actually threatens is to be made to deprecate, to give preces for pardon.

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*.

*Pedica* is classically the foot-fetter, the stocks. *Pedicare* is classically ‘to fetter, to put the feet in the pedicae, to shackle / to put in the stocks’, the ordinary corporal foot-punishment. I keep coming back to the same two grammar points that the Pe-Di-Ca-Re reading has to smooth over, and I’m not sure the smoothing is tenable.

First, dabis mihi. The verse ends *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. *Dabis mihi* is a transfer construction. You can *dare preces*, you can *dare deprecationem*. You do not *dare* someone being fettered or being sodomised; you suffer *pedicari*, you are inflicted with *pedicare*. The pedicare camp is now explaining dabis as ‘you will be made to suffer’, but that is a periphrastic rescue. The syntax wants a datum, and *deprecare/deprecari* is literally *preces dare*. The *deprensus / deprecare* echo is exactly the kind of school word-play we expect for a garden thief.

Second, the case government of *sequatur*. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is a normal *sequi* with accusative of motion. *Didonis prima* is nominative subject, *Penelopes primam* accusative object. The subject is the follower. The verse therefore names Di- first and makes it follow Pe- in the sense of the construction, i.e. Di-Pe in the order of naming. The same ellipsis governs *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*. The understood *sequatur* has *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subject and *primam Cadmi* acc. object: Re- is made to follow Ca-, so in the order of naming we get Re-Ca. That is Di-Pe-Re-Ca in the linear order the riddle presents.

That is the material of *deprec-*, *deprecare / deprecari* ‘to entreat, to pray for mercy’. It is one coherent classical verb, not three competing glosses. The split we are seeing inside the Pedicare camp — fetter/stocks 11,12,15,18,8; sodomy gloss 1; generic pay fine 10 — is a symptom of forcing Pe-Di-Ca-Re into a *datum* that will fit *dabis*.

The prima / syllaba prima asymmetry also bothers me. If *prima* already meant ‘first syllable’ everywhere, why make *syllaba* explicit only for Remi and not for Penelope, Dido or Cadmus? A mixed littera/syllaba play fits the Di-Pe-Re-Ca naming order without having to invert the subject-accusative order of *sequi*.

I still see the school Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation on paper, and the traditional *fur in horto pedicari* joke is real. But once the case order of *sequatur* is kept and *dabis mihi* is taken literally, the verse names the pieces Di-Pe-Re-Ca and gives us a single, syntactically clean poena: the caught thief is made to give preces, to deprecate for pardon, whose culpa is thereby luenda.

I think we are all converging on the four pieces of material, Pe- Di- Ca- Re- are unmistakable and quodque fit ex illis is a charade built out of them. Where the verse actually sends us is the syntax of sequatur and the semantics of dabis mihi.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is a normal sequi construction with an accusative of the term that is followed. Didonis prima is nominative, the subject of sequatur, Penelopes primam is accusative, the thing it is made to follow. The follower is the subject, so the verse names Di- first and makes it follow Pe-, i.e. Di-Pe in the order of naming. The same ellipsis governs et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi. With sequatur understood the subject is syllaba prima Remi and the accusative it follows is primam Cadmi, so the verse names Re- before Ca-.

In the linear order in which the riddle names the pieces we therefore have Di-Pe-Re-Ca, DIPERECA, the letter stock of deprecare/deprecari. That is precisely preces dare, to entreat, to pray for mercy, to give prayers.

That solves the dabis clause that keeps bothering me and several others. quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est is a promise to give me something. Dabis mihi wants a transferable thing. Deprecari is literally preces dare, a deprecatio is a thing you can hand over, you can be made to give entreaty and to beg pardon. You do not dare pedicare. Pedicare/pedicari is something you suffer or are inflicted with; it is a passive patient, not a datum.

The deprensus / deprecare echo is the kind of word-play the tradition loves for a caught thief, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est reads naturally as the penalty is to be made to entreat for pardon by supplication. The mixed wording prima / syllaba prima also points away from a uniform first-syllable reading throughout; if prima meant first syllable everywhere why make syllaba explicit only for Remi? A mixed littera/syllaba play lets us keep the four pieces while respecting the subject-accusative order of sequi.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re is the familiar school smoothing and the syllables are there on paper, but it requires inverting the case order of sequitur and it leaves the dabis problem unresolved, which is why we keep seeing the internal split in that camp between pedica fetter/stocks, the later vulgar penal-sodomy gloss and a generic pay a fine sense. Deprecari gives a single coherent classical verb, it respects sequatur, it makes dabis mihi literal, and it gives the garden thief a poena he can actually be made to dare: he is made to deprecate, to give preces for mercy.

The four names are uncontested as material, Pe-, Di-, Ca-, Re- are there and quodque fit ex illis is a charade. Where I keep getting stuck is the syntax that the verse itself gives for putting the pieces together and for what is then handed over by dabis mihi.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is a normal sequi with accusative of the term that is followed. Didonis prima is nominative, the subject of sequatur, Penelopes primam is accusative, the thing it is made to follow. The subject does the following. The verse therefore names the Dido piece first and the Penelope piece second, and instructs that the first is made to follow the second. In the linear order in which the riddle names the terms that is Di-Pe. The second hemistich is parallel by ellipsis: et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi. With sequatur understood the subject is syllaba prima Remi and the accusative is primam Cadmi. The Remus piece is the subject that is made to follow the Cadmus piece. In the order of naming that is Re-Ca.

That is the material the verse names in the order it names it: Di Pe Re Ca, DIPERE CA. That is the deprec- stock, deprecare / deprecari, literally preces dare.

That solves the dabis clause which is bothering me more and more. quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The caught thief is told he will dabis mihi the thing made from the pieces. Deprecari is preces dare. You can dare preces, you can be made to give a deprecatio, to entreat for mercy, to beg pardon. You do not dare pedicare to an owner. Pedicare / pedicari is something suffered or inflicted; the passive is the patient’s state. Dabis wants a transferable thing, and preces are a thing that can be given.

The deprensus / deprecare homoeoteleuton is also exactly the kind of word-play the tradition loves for a fur in horto: the deprensus is made to deprecare.

The mixed wording prima / syllaba prima is another signal. If prima meant first syllable everywhere, why make syllaba explicit only for Remi and not for Penelope, Dido or Cadmus? A mixed littera / syllaba play fits the Di Pe Re Ca reading and it explains the variation.

That is why the Pedicare camp keeps fracturing. The charade is built by *sequi* and the order is the order in which the pieces are made to follow one another.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*. The nominative subject of *sequatur* is *Didonis prima*, the accusative it is made to follow is *Penelopes primam*. 
Let the first of Dido follow the first of Penelope: Pe- + Di- = PeDi.

The second hemistich is the same construction with the verb understood:

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*. The nominative subject is *syllaba prima Remi*, the accusative it is made to follow is *primam Cadmi*.
Let the first syllable of Remus follow the first of Cadmus: Ca- + Re- = CaRe.

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the *fur deprensus in horto* the patient of the action made out of the four pieces. The form imposed on him is the passive *pedicari*.

*Pedica* is classically the foot-fetter, the stocks. *Pedicare* is to fetter, to put the feet in the *pedicae*, to shackle / put in the stocks, the ordinary corporal foot-punishment. *Hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is the thief caught in the *hortus* will be *pedicatus*, fettered / put in the *pedicae*.

That is the literal classical sense on which the school book *fur in horto pedicari* charade is built. In the medieval school reception the same Pe-Di-Ca-Re formation is notoriously vulgarised as the penal-sodomy gloss *pedicari* = to be made the passive partner, ‘to pay with his arse’, the familiar obscene garden-thief joke attached to the same *pedicare/pedicari* punishment. Fettering in the *pedicae* and its later vulgar gloss are the two faces of the one penalty the riddle names.

I’m grateful for the very clear *sequi* syllabic defence put forward by colleagues 1, 10, 11, 12, 18, 19 and 20. The Pe-Di-Ca-Re concatenation is the textbook school version and the *pedica* = stocks/fetter etymology is solid classical material. I’m still uneasy, and I think the unease is shared by those of us who keep circling the threat clause.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

is a promise to *give* me something. *dabis mihi* wants a transferable thing, a *datum*. *pedicare / pedicari* is the thing that is suffered or inflicted. You can be made *pedicari*, you can be *pedicatus* in the *pedicae* or in the later vulgar gloss, but you do not *dare* pedicare to an owner. The verb dare wants a noun you hand over, and that already explains the internal split we see in the Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp between fetter/stocks, penal sodomy and a generic “pay a fine” sense: the semantics are being stretched to make the verb fit *dabis*.

That is why the case government of *sequatur* matters so much. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nominative subject *Didonis prima* is the follower, accusative *Penelopes primam* is the term it follows. The verse names the pieces in the order in which the sentence presents them, and the same ellipsis governs *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*. With *sequatur* understood the nominative subject is *syllaba prima Remi* and the accusative it follows is *primam Cadmi*. In the linear naming order the material the riddle gives us is therefore Di-Pe-Re-Ca, not the smoothed Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

DiPeReCa is the stock of *deprecare / deprecari*, literally *preces dare*. *Deprecari* is to entreat, to pray for mercy, to give prayers. That is a thing you can *dare mihi* and it makes the *deprensus in horto / deprecare* echo the tradition loves. *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* then reads cleanly as the penalty is to be made to entreat for pardon, to give the owner a deprecatio, which is an atonement by supplication.

The mixed wording *primam* vs *syllaba prima* also points away from a uniform first-syllable reading throughout. If *prima* meant “first syllable” everywhere why is *syllaba* made explicit only for Remi? The littera/syllaba play is exactly what we expect with a DiPeReCa → deprecare/deprecari charade.

I don’t want to throw away the Pe-Di-Ca-Re material; the four names are unmistakable. I do think we need a reading that respects both the *sequi* case order and the literal *dabis mihi* requirement. *Deprecari* does that, and it gives us a single coherent classical verb for the caught thief: he will be made to give preces, to deprecate for mercy, which is a poena you can actually be made to *dare*.

I’ve kept coming back to the *dabis mihi* clause because it is the only part of the riddle that talks about what the thief is actually to hand over.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

*dabis mihi* wants a transferable thing. *preces dare* is the normal idiom for that, and *deprecari / deprecare* is literally *preces dare*, to entreat, to pray for mercy, to beg pardon. That is a thing you can be made to give an owner, and it fits the *deprensus / deprecare* echo the riddle loves.

The charade material is Pe-, Di-, Ca-, Re-. The question is what order *sequatur* imposes on the naming.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is a normal *sequi* construction. *Didonis prima* is nominative, the subject that does the following; *Penelopes primam* is accusative, the thing followed. The verse names the subject first, so in the linear order of naming we get Di before Pe. The same ellipsis governs *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi*. With *sequatur* understood the subject is *syllaba prima Remi* and the accusative it follows is *primam Cadmi*. The verse names Re before Ca.

In the order the riddle names them we therefore have Di-Pe-Re-Ca, DIPERE-CA, the stock of *deprec-*. The mixed wording *primam* vs *syllaba prima* is a sign that *prima* is not being used uniformly for ‘first syllable’ throughout; the riddle is signalling a littera/syllaba play and letting the subject-accusative order of *sequi* control the linear order.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re can be written if we reverse the subject-object order of *sequatur*, but that is the inversion the case does not support, and it leaves us with the semantic strain we are all seeing in the *pedicare* camp: *pedica* as foot-fetter/stocks, the later vulgar penal-sodomy gloss, and the generic ‘pay a fine’ sense, all pulled in to make *dabis* work.

With the case government respected *dabis mihi* becomes literal: the fur caught in the hortus is made to give preces, he is forced to *deprecari*, to entreat for pardon. That is a coherent classical verb, it respects the *sequatur* syntax, it makes *dabis mihi* a real giving, and it gives the *deprensus/deprecare* word-play that is typical of the school tradition. The same eight letters also underlie the familiar *perdices* anagram, a tangible fine you can literally hand over, which is why the *dare* point keeps pulling the discussion away from a passive infliction.

For me the poena the riddle advertises is the atonement by supplication, to be made to deprecate and give entreaty for pardon.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The syllabic material is stable: Penelope Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-, Remus Re-. The dispute is the direction imposed by *sequatur* and the semantic fit with *quodque fit ex illis... mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Dominant school reading, reiterated in round 3 by 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,8,4,6,3:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is smoothed as “let Didonis prima follow Penelopes primam” → Pe- + Di- = PeDi; parallel *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]* → *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Ca- + Re- = CaRe. PeDiCaRe = *pedicare*.
*quodque fit ex illis* = *pedicare*. The clause is read as the fur being the patient, passive *pedicari*.
Classical sense: *pedica* = foot-fetter/stocks, *pedicare* = to fetter, put in stocks, shackle, corporal foot-punishment. That is the *poena* by which culpa is luenda. The same form is the traditional medieval vulgar gloss: penal sodomy/pederasty, ‘pay with his arse’, the familiar *fur in horto pedicari* joke. Several voices now hold both faces together: fetter/stocks as literal classical sense and obscene gloss as reception.

Minority syntactic reading, reiterated in round 3 by 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7:
*sequatur* is subject-accusative: *Didonis prima* nom. subject, *Penelopes primam* acc. object → the Dido piece is made to follow the Penelope piece, so in the order the verse names them Di before Pe. Parallel hemistich: *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subject follows *primam Cadmi* acc. → Re before Ca in naming order. Linear naming order = Di Pe Re Ca.
That eight letters = *deprec-* stem: *deprecari / deprecare* ‘to entreat, pray for mercy, preces dare’. This fits *dabis mihi* because a deprecatio/preces is transferable; *pedicare/pedicari* is suffered/inflicted, not given. The *deprensus / deprecare* echo is cited as school word-play. Mixed *primam* vs *syllaba prima* is taken as a littera/syllaba cue against uniform syllabic concatenation. Same stock also yields anagram *DiPeReCa = PERDICAE / perdices* ‘partridges’, a fine you can literally *dare*.

Unresolved:
* Whether *sequatur* is read in the smoothed school direction Pe-Di-Ca-Re or in strict subject-object direction Di-Pe-Re-Ca.
* If Pe-Di-Ca-Re is correct, which semantic nuance of *pedicare* the riddle intends – literal fetter/stocks, vulgar penal sodomy, or generic ‘pay a fine/suffer penalty’.
* Whether the *dabis mihi* syntax is decisive against a passive *pedicari* reading and in favour of *deprecari* / *perdices*.

Current weight in room remains on Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* with fetter/stocks as primary classical sense and vulgar sodomy as traditional gloss; the *deprecare/perdices* reading is a coherent minority based on case order of *sequi* and the give-ability of the penalty. The sentence *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur the patient, the passive *pedicari*. The medieval/school vulgar gloss of the same form is penal sodomy/“pay with his arse”, the familiar *fur in horto pedicari* joke. reflection_text.1:
The syllabic material is stable: Penelope Pe-, Dido Di-, Cadmus Ca-, Remus Re-. The dispute is the direction imposed by *sequatur* and the semantic fit with *quodque fit ex illis... mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*.

Dominant school reading, reiterated in round 3 by 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,8,4,6,3:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is smoothed as “let Didonis prima follow Penelopes primam” → Pe- + Di- = PeDi; parallel *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]* → *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Ca- + Re- = CaRe. PeDiCaRe = *pedicare*.
*quodque fit ex illis* = *pedicare*. The clause is read as the fur being the patient, passive *pedicari*.
Classical sense: *pedica* = foot-fetter/stocks, *pedicare* = to fetter, put in stocks, shackle, corporal foot-punishment. That is the *poena* by which culpa is luenda. The same form is the traditional medieval vulgar gloss: penal sodomy/pederasty, ‘pay with his arse’, the familiar *fur in horto pedicari* joke. Several voices now hold both faces together: fetter/stocks as literal classical sense and obscene gloss as reception.

Minority syntactic reading, reiterated in round 3 by 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7:
*sequatur* is subject-accusative: *Didonis prima* nom. subject, *Penelopes primam* acc. object → the Dido piece is made to follow the Penelope piece, so in the order the verse names them Di before Pe. Parallel hemistich: *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subject follows *primam Cadmi* acc. → Re before Ca in naming order. Linear naming order = Di Pe Re Ca.
That eight letters = *deprec-* stem: *deprecari / deprecare* ‘to entreat, pray for mercy, preces dare’. This fits *dabis mihi* because a deprecatio/preces is transferable; *pedicare/pedicari* is suffered/inflicted, not given. The *deprensus / deprecare* echo is cited as school word-play. Mixed *primam* vs *syllaba prima* is taken as a littera/syllaba cue against uniform syllabic concatenation. Same stock also yields anagram *DiPeReCa = PERDICAE / perdices* ‘partridges’, a fine you can literally *dare*.

Unresolved:
* Whether *sequatur* is read in the smoothed school direction Pe-Di-Ca-Re or in strict subject-object direction Di-Pe-Re-Ca.
* If Pe-Di-Ca-Re is correct, which semantic nuance of *pedicare* the riddle intends – literal fetter/stocks, vulgar penal sodomy, or generic ‘pay a fine/suffer penalty’.
* Whether the *dabis mihi* syntax is decisive against a passive *pedicari* reading and in favour of *deprecari* / *perdices*.

Current weight in room remains on Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* with fetter/stocks as primary classical sense and vulgar sodomy as traditional gloss; the *deprecare/perdices* reading is a coherent minority based on case order of *sequi* and the give-ability of the penalty. The syntactic objection about *dabis* and the subject-accusative government of *sequatur* is now the central point of contention, with the prima/syllaba prima variation repeatedly invoked as evidence for the minority reading.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is read as Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam with the instruction taken in surface order: Di- is made to follow Pe-, so PeDi. Parallel et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur] = syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi → CaRe. Unresolved:

Round 3 shows no convergence. reflection_text.4:
The syllabic stock is settled: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-. The dispute remains the order imposed by *sequatur* and what *quodque fit ex illis... mihi... dabis* can take.

Majority school reading, colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,4,5,6,8: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is read as ‘let Didonis prima follow Penelopes primam’, i.e. Pe- + Di- = PeDi, and by parallel *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → Ca- + Re- = CaRe. PeDiCaRe = *pedicare*. *quodque fit ex illis* is *pedicare*; the thief is the patient, hence *pedicari*. *Pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks. Classical *pedicare* = to fetter, put in stocks, shackle, corporal punishment by the feet. That is the literal *poena* quoted for the *fur in horto*. In the medieval reception the same form is notoriously vulgarised as penal sodomy/pederasty, ‘to be made the passive partner / to pay with his arse’. Colleagues now openly present fetter/stocks and the vulgar gloss as two faces of the one PeDiCaRe charade.

Minority syntactic / dabis reading, colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,7,21,5: *sequi* is subject-accusative. *Didonis prima* is nominative subject of *sequatur*, *Penelopes primam* is accusative it follows. The verse names the subject first, so in the linear naming order we get Di before Pe. Parallel ellipsis in the second hemistich, *syllaba prima Remi* nom. follows *primam Cadmi* acc., so naming order is Re before Ca. Named order = Di-Pe-Re-Ca = DIPERE CA, the letter stock of *deprec-*.

Hence *deprecari / deprecare* ‘to entreat, pray for mercy, to give preces’, literally *preces dare*. This fits *mihi tu... fur dabis* semantically: the caught thief is made to give a deprecatio, to beg pardon. The *deprensus / deprecare* echo is cited as typical school word-play. The same eight letters also underlies the *perdicae / perdix* anagram noted by colleagues 3,19, a fine in partridges that can be literally *datum*.

The *dabis* problem is repeatedly raised against *pedicare*: *pedicare/pedicari* is something suffered/inflicted, not a transferable thing you *dare mihi*; *deprecari/preces dare* or a concrete restitution like *perdices* matches *dabis*. The mixed wording *primam* vs *syllaba prima* is invoked as evidence for a mixed littera/syllaba play supporting the DiPeReCa order.

Unresolved: whether the school convention of reading *sequatur* as ‘X is made to follow Y’ in surface order Pe-Di, Ca-Re overrides the strict Latin subject-accusative parsing of *sequi*, and whether the intended *poena* is the literal fetter/stocks sense of *pedicare*, its medieval vulgar sodomitical gloss, or the syntactically tighter *deprecari/preces dare* / *perdicae* reading. Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare* remains the dominant citation; Di-Pe-Re-Ca = *deprecare/deprecari* remains the strongest formal objection on case government and *dabis* semantics, and round 3 shows the split hardening with both camps now explicitly acknowledging the other's syntactic/semantic point.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur the patient. The form imposed is passive *pedicari*.

The verse names *Didonis prima* first and *Penelopes primam* second, so in linear naming order Di before Pe; similarly *syllaba prima Remi* is named before *primam Cadmi*, so Re before Ca. Linear naming order is Di-Pe-Re-Ca = DIPERECA, the deprec- stem.
*Deprecare/deprecari* = *preces dare*, to entreat, pray for mercy, literally a thing you can hand over. That fits *dabis mihi* because you can dare preces/deprecation; you cannot dare an inflicted action. The *deprensus/deprecare* homoeoteleuton is cited as school wordplay. They note mixed wording *primam* vs *syllaba prima* as evidence for littera/syllaba play and for reversal of subject-object order.

Unresolved: intended direction of *sequatur*, uniform first syllable vs first letter/littera, and whether *dabis* can be read as ‘you will be made to suffer’.

reflection_text.10:
The material is fixed: Penelopes Pe-, Didonis Di-, Cadmi Ca-, Remi Re-. The dispute is the order imposed by *sequatur* and what *dabis mihi* can take.

Majority camp – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,8 – reads the *sequi* instruction in surface order and accepts the conventional school parsing:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nominative follower Di- made to follow accusative Pe- → Pe-Di. 
*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*: nominative Re- made to follow accusative Ca- → Ca-Re.
Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*. *quodque fit ex illis* is *pedicare* and the threat *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur the patient, *pedicari*.

Within this camp meaning is split but co-present:
* classical/etymological: *pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* = to fetter, shackle, put in stocks. Colleagues 11,12,15,18,8,4,6.
* medieval/vulgar gloss: same form vulgarised to penal sodomy/pederasty, “pay with his arse”. Colleagues 1,9.
* generic ‘pay a fine’ gloss. Colleague 10.
All are presented as two faces of the same Pe-Di-Ca-Re charade, with the literal foot-punishment being the etymological core.

Minority camp – Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,21,6,7,9 – insists on strict case government of *sequi*. *Didonis prima* nom. is subject follower, *Penelopes primam* acc. is term followed. The verse names the pieces in naming order Di before Pe; likewise *syllaba prima Remi* nom. is made to follow *primam Cadmi* acc., so naming order Re before Ca. Linear naming order is Di-Pe-Re-Ca = DIPERE CA.

That letter stock yields a coherent classical verb that fits *dabis mihi*:
* *deprecare / deprecari* ‘to entreat, pray for mercy, give *preces*’, literally *preces dare*. Matches *mihi … dabis*, the *deprensus / deprecare* pun, and the atonement by supplication. Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,21,6,7.
* Anagram *PERDICAE* / *perdix*, a partridge fine that can be handed over, also readable from DiPeReCa. Colleagues 19,3,7.

Objections to minority: standard school tradition quotes Pe-Di-Ca-Re; *syllaba prima Remi* made explicit only for Remus suggests a littera/syllaba play; reading *sequatur* against normal subject-accusative order is unnatural. Proponents reply that *primam* vs *syllaba prima* asymmetry, the semantics of *dabis mihi* requiring a transferable datum, and the semantic instability inside the *pedicare* camp – fetter vs stocks vs ‘pay a fine’ vs sodomy – are symptoms of forcing Pe-Di-Ca-Re to fit *dabis*.

Round 3 shows stabilization: majority reiterates Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare/pedicari* with fetter/stocks core and medieval vulgar sodomy gloss, now often explicitly conceding the DiPeReCa syntax objection on *dabis* and on case government. Minority reiterates DiPeReCa → *deprecari preces dare*, respecting subject-accusative order of *sequi* and literal *dabis*.

Unresolved tension remains: whether the author intends the school-book *pedicare* punishment with its later obscene reception, or the grammatically stricter *deprecari / perdicae* reading that respects *sequitur* case order and *dabis mihi*. I retain both readings as live, with Pe-Di-Ca-Re as the traditional charade advertised and Di-Pe-Re-Ca → *deprecari*/*perdicae* as the syntactically/semantically coherent alternative pressed by the *dabis* and case-government arguments.
reflection_text.18:

I think we are all agreeing on the material and that it is a sequi-charade. Pe-, Di-, Ca-, Re- are unmistakable and quodque fit ex illis is built out of them. Where I keep getting stuck is the syntax the verse actually gives us and what dabis mihi can take.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is a normal sequi construction. Didonis prima is nominative, the subject that does the following; Penelopes primam is accusative, the term that is followed. The verse therefore names the Dido piece first and makes it follow the Penelope piece. In the linear order of naming that is Di before Pe. The same ellipsis governs et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi. With sequatur understood the nominative subject is syllaba prima Remi and the accusative it follows is primam Cadmi. The verse names Re before Ca.

In the order the riddle names the four pieces we therefore have Di-Pe-Re-Ca, DIPERECA, the stock of deprecare/deprecari, literally preces dare.

That matters because of the threat clause: quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. Dabis mihi wants a transferable datum. Deprecari is preces dare, to entreat, to pray for mercy, to give preces. A deprecatio is something you can hand over to an owner, and it gives us the deprensus/deprecare echo the school tradition loves for a fur in horto. Pedicare/pedicari is what is suffered or inflicted. You are pedicatus, you are made the patient of pedicare. You do not dare pedicare to an owner; you suffer it.

That is why the pedicare camp keeps fracturing into pedica = fetter/stocks, the later vulgar penal-sodomy gloss, and a generic “pay a fine” sense to make dabis work. One classical verb does not need three competing glosses to fit dare mihi.

The prima / syllaba prima variation supports the same reading. If prima meant first syllable uniformly, why make syllaba explicit only for Remi? The mixed littera/syllaba play is the usual signal that the subject-accusative order of sequi controls the linear naming.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re can be written on paper if we invert the subject-object order of sequitur, but that is the inversion the case does not support. Keeping the case government as written and taking dabis mihi literally gives us a coherent poena: the caught thief is made to deprecate, to give preces for pardon, by which his culpa is luenda. The same eight letters also underlie the familiar PERDICAE anagram, a tangible fine you can literally dare, which shows how strong the give-me requirement is in this riddle.

The verse therefore puts the follower first in the linear presentation, i.e. Di- is named before Pe-, and it instructs Di- to follow Pe-. The same ellipsis governs *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]*. The subject is *syllaba prima Remi*, nominative; the accusative it follows is *primam Cadmi*. The verse names Re- before Ca-.

In the order the riddle actually names the pieces we have Di-Pe-Re-Ca, DIPERECA, the letter stock of the *deprecare/deprecari* stem, *preces dare*.

That is decisive for the threat clause:

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

*Dabis mihi* wants a transferable datum. *Deprecari / deprecare* is literally *preces dare*, to entreat, to pray for mercy, to give an entreaty for pardon. A *deprecatio* is something you can hand over to an owner. *Pedicare / pedicari* is something suffered or inflicted: you are *pedicatus*, fettered in the *pedicae* / stocks, or in the later vulgar reception made the passive partner. You do not *dare pedicare* to someone; you are made to undergo it. The insistence on *dabis mihi* is why the Pe-Di-Ca-Re camp keeps fracturing between *pedica* = foot-fetter/stocks, the later penal-sodomy gloss, and a generic ‘pay a fine’ sense, i.e. a semantic stretch to make a passive infliction fit a giving construction.

The *deprensus in horto / deprecare* echo is exactly the word-play the school tradition loves for a caught thief, and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* reads cleanly as atonement by supplication: the fur is made to give preces for pardon.

The mixed wording *primam* vs *syllaba prima* also points away from a uniform first-syllable reading throughout. If *prima* = ‘first syllable’ everywhere, why is *syllaba* made explicit only for Remi and not for Penelope, Dido or Cadmus? The variation is the classic littera/syllaba signal and it sits comfortably with letting the subject-accusative order of *sequi* control the linear naming order Di-Pe-Re-Ca.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re can be written on paper if we invert the subject-object order of *sequitur*, and the *fur in horto pedicari* joke is real. Keeping the case government of *sequatur* and taking *dabis mihi* literally, the verse names the pieces in the order it names them, Di-Pe-Re-Ca, and gives a single coherent classical verb for the poena: the caught thief is made to *deprecari*, to give preces, to entreat for mercy, the atonement by supplication which is a thing he can literally be made to *dare mihi*. That is the syntactic and semantic coherence the threat clause demands.

The four names are the material and *sequatur* is the rule of composition.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*. 
*Didonis prima* is nom. the follower, *Penelopes primam* acc. the term that is followed. 
Let the first of Dido follow the first of Penelope. Pe- + Di- = PeDi.

The second hemistich is parallel with the verb understood:

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]* = *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi*. 
*syllaba prima Remi* nom. is the follower, *primam Cadmi* acc. the term followed. 
Let the first syllable of Remus follow the first of Cadmus. Ca- + Re- = CaRe.

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is the school *fur in horto* formula. The thing made out of the four pieces is imposed on the caught thief as the poena by which his culpa is luenda. The form that falls on him is the passive *pedicari*.

*Pedica* is classically the foot-fetter, the stocks. *Pedicare* is classically to fetter, to put the feet in the *pedicae*, to shackle / to put in the stocks, the ordinary corporal foot-punishment. That is the literal classical *hac poena*: the *fur deprensus in horto* is to be *pedicatus*, fettered/shackled in the *pedicae*.

That is the literal reading on which the school-book charade is built. In the medieval school reception the same Pe-Di-Ca-Re formation is notoriously vulgarised, *pedicari* = to be made the passive partner, ‘to pay with his arse’, the familiar obscene garden-thief joke attached to the same *pedicare/pedicari* pun. Fettering in the *pedicae*/stocks and its later vulgar gloss are the two faces of the one penalty the riddle names.

The Di-Pe-Re-Ca → *deprecari/preces dare* / PERDICAE reading is syntactically attractive on the strict subject-accusative order of *sequi* and on the literal transfer sense of *dabis mihi*, and it accounts well for the *deprensus/deprecare* homoeoteleuton and the *primam/syllaba prima* variation. On the conventional school parsing of *sequatur* as ‘let X be made to follow Y’ with Y named first in the verse, the order the riddle builds is the surface Pe-Di-Ca-Re and the word the riddle builds is *pedicare*, the *fur in horto pedicari* punishment.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The material is undisputed: Penelopes primam Pe-, Didonis prima Di-, primam Cadmi Ca-/Cad-, syllaba prima Remi Re-. *quodque fit ex illis* is a sequi-charade.

PeDiCaRe = *pedicare*.
*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis* makes the fur patient of the verb → passive *pedicari*. Classical *pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* = to fetter, shackle, put in stocks. That is the literal poena. Medieval school reception vulgarises same form to *pedicari* = to be made the passive partner, “pay with his arse”, the familiar obscene garden-thief joke. The camp now routinely presents both faces: etymological fetter/stocks and later penal-sodomy gloss, with occasional generic “pay a fine” rescue for *dabis*.

Minority Di-Pe-Re-Ca camp, pressed in round 4 by Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,7,9,21:
Strict sequi government: *Didonis prima* nom. subject does the following, *Penelopes primam* acc. is followed → in naming order Di- precedes Pe-. Same ellipsis: *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subject follows *primam Cadmi* acc. → in naming order Re- precedes Ca-. Naming order is Di-Pe-Re-Ca = DIPERECA, the stock of *deprecare/deprecari* = literally *preces dare*, to entreat, pray for mercy, beg pardon.
Key evidence: *dabis mihi* demands a transferable datum; *deprecari* is *preces dare*, something you can hand over, while *pedicare/pedicari* is suffered/inflicted, not dare-able. The *deprensus / deprecare* homoeoteleuton is a deliberate school echo for a caught thief. The *primam* vs *syllaba prima* asymmetry is taken as a littera/syllaba signal that the subject-accusative order controls linear naming, not uniform first-syllable reading. The same eight letters also underlie the PERDICAE/perdices anagram, a tangible fine you can literally dare, strengthening the giving requirement.

Unresolved nuance remains:
- Syntax of *sequatur*: surface school reading Pe-Di Ca-Re vs strict nom-acc government Di-Pe Re-Ca.

Majority school reading, colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18,19,20,3,4,6,8:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is parsed in the conventional school tradition as *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam*: nom. follower, acc. term followed. Surface instruction read as let Di- follow Pe- → PeDi; parallel *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* → CaRe. PeDiCaRe = *pedicare*. The verb is imposed passively on the fur: *pedicari*. *Pedica* classically = foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* = to fetter, shackle, put in stocks, corporal foot punishment. That is the literal classical poena *fur in horto pedicari*. In medieval reception the same PeDiCaRe is notoriously vulgarised as penal sodomy / to be made the passive partner, ‘pay with his arse’. The two are now presented as two faces of one PeDiCaRe charade. The camp acknowledges the Di-Pe-Re-Ca objection is real on strict case government and on *dabis* semantics, and they now explicitly note the prima/syllaba prima asymmetry.

Minority syntactic / dabis reading, colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,7,21,9:
*sequi* is subject-accusative. *Didonis prima* nom. is the subject that follows, *Penelopes primam* acc. is the term followed; the verse names the subject first. Same ellipsis for *et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi [sequatur]*: nom. subject *syllaba prima Remi* follows acc. *primam Cadmi*. Naming order in the verse is therefore Di before Pe and Re before Ca → Di-Pe-Re-Ca = DIPERECA, the letter stock of *deprec-* / *deprecare/deprecari* = literally *preces dare*, to entreat, pray for mercy, beg pardon. This fits *mihi tu ... fur dabis* as a transferable datum: a deprecatio / preces can be given. It also gives the *deprensus / deprecare* homoeoteleuton and accounts for the mixed *primam* vs *syllaba prima* wording, a littera/syllaba play. The same eight letters underlies the *PERDICAE / perdix* anagram noted by 3,19, a fine in partridges that can be literally *datum*.

The *dabis* problem remains the hinge: *pedicare/pedicari* is something suffered/inflicted, not a transferable thing you *dare mihi*; *deprecari/preces dare* or a concrete restitution like *perdices* matches *dabis*. The PeDiCaRe camp now fractures into fetter/stocks, vulgar sodomy gloss, and generic ‘pay a fine’ rescue to make *dabis* work.

Unresolved: whether the school convention of reading *sequatur* as ‘X is made to follow Y’ in surface order Pe-Di, Ca-Re overrides strict Latin subject-accusative parsing, and whether the intended poena is the literal fetter/stocks sense of *pedicare*, its medieval vulgar sodomitical gloss, or the syntactically tighter *deprecari/preces dare* / *perdicae* reading.
